# Test Scripts, Debugging, and Data-Driven Testing in Postman: The Complete Workflow I Rely On There's a specific moment in my API testing journey where things shifted from "manually clicking Send and eyeballing the response" to "actually running a test suite." That shift happened once I got serious about three things: writing real test scripts, debugging them properly when they failed, and feeding them data instead of hardcoded values. This post is my full walkthrough of all three, in the order I actually learned them, with the diagrams, tested code, and hard-won lessons I picked up along the way. --- ## Table of Contents 1. [Why Test Scripts Changed How I Work](#why-test-scripts-changed-how-i-work) 2. [The `pm.test()` Powerhouse](#the-pmtest-powerhouse) 3. [Setting Variables From Responses](#setting-variables-from-responses) 4. [Basic If/Else Logic in Tests](#basic-ifelse-logic-in-tests) 5. [My First Real End-to-End Test](#my-first-real-end-to-end-test) 6. [Reading Test Results in Postman](#reading-test-results-in-postman) 7. [Debugging: Why Half My Time Goes Here](#debugging-why-half-my-time-goes-here) 8. [The Console Is My Best Friend](#the-console-is-my-best-friend) 9. [Isolating the Problem](#isolating-the-problem) 10. [Scrutinizing the Response](#scrutinizing-the-response) 11. [Thinking Like a Scientist](#thinking-like-a-scientist) 12. [A Full Debugging Walkthrough](#a-full-debugging-walkthrough) 13. [Advanced Debugging Tools](#advanced-debugging-tools) 14. [Why I Moved to Data-Driven Testing](#why-i-moved-to-data-driven-testing) 15. [CSV vs. JSON as Data Sources](#csv-vs-json-as-data-sources) 16. [Running Data Through the Collection Runner](#running-data-through-the-collection-runner) 17. [Writing Data-Aware Tests](#writing-data-aware-tests) 18. [Managing Large Datasets](#managing-large-datasets) 19. [Generating Test Data Dynamically](#generating-test-data-dynamically) 20. [Reporting on Data-Driven Results](#reporting-on-data-driven-results) 21. [The Full Workflow, Visualized](#the-full-workflow-visualized) 22. [Mistakes I Made Along the Way](#mistakes-i-made-along-the-way) 23. [Wrapping Up](#wrapping-up) --- ## Why Test Scripts Changed How I Work For a while, "testing" an API meant sending a request and looking at the response with my own eyes. That works fine for one request, once. It falls apart completely the moment I need to check the same thing fifty times, or make sure a fix didn't break something else three weeks from now. Test scripts fixed that. A script I write once keeps checking the same thing forever, consistently, without me needing to remember what "correct" looked like last time. | Before Test Scripts | After Test Scripts | | --- | --- | | Manually eyeballing each response | Automated pass/fail assertions | | Forgetting what "correct" looked like | A documented, repeatable expectation | | No record of what passed/failed | Green checkmarks and red X's, saved per run | | Re-checking everything by hand after a change | Re-running the whole suite in seconds | --- ## The `pm.test()` Powerhouse Everything starts with `pm.test()`. It's the single most-used line in my entire testing workflow. ```javascript pm.test("Status code is 200", function () { pm.response.to.have.status(200); }); ``` Breaking down the anatomy: - `pm.test(name, fn)` — registers a named test; the name shows up in the Tests tab - Inside the function, I use Postman's built-in assertions — `pm.response.to.have.status(200)` checks the status code specifically I tested this exact pattern against a live endpoint: ```bash curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://reqres.in/api/users/2" ``` Output: ``` 200 ``` Which confirms the assertion above would pass. > **Note:** Postman's assertion syntax is built on [Chai.js](https://www.chaijs.com/), a JavaScript assertion library. If something in `pm.expect(...)` looks unfamiliar, searching "chai assertion \[thing\]" usually gets me an answer faster than searching Postman docs directly. --- ## Setting Variables From Responses The second pattern I leaned on constantly: extract something from a response and store it for later use. ```javascript pm.test("User creation successful", function () { pm.response.to.have.status(201); let jsonData = pm.response.json(); pm.environment.set("newUserId", jsonData.id); }); ``` Tested against Reqres: ```bash curl -s -X POST "https://reqres.in/api/users" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"name": "Casey", "job": "QA Analyst"}' ``` Response: ```json { "name": "Casey", "job": "QA Analyst", "id": "331", "createdAt": "2026-09-24T08:12:03.552Z" } ``` That `id` value is exactly what gets captured by `jsonData.id` and stored for the next request in the chain. --- ## Basic If/Else Logic in Tests Not every response looks the same, so I branch my test logic based on what actually came back: ```javascript pm.test("Error handling", function () { if (pm.response.code === 400) { pm.test("Bad Request error is shown", () => { const data = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(data).to.have.property("error"); }); } else { pm.test("Request succeeded", () => { pm.response.to.have.status(200); }); } }); ``` > **Caution:** Nesting `pm.test()` calls inside each other (as shown above) works, but I keep it shallow — one level of nesting at most. Deeply nested tests get confusing fast, both to read and to debug when something fails. --- ## My First Real End-to-End Test Here's the scenario that finally made everything click for me: testing a product search endpoint. ### Scenario - **Endpoint:** `GET /products` - **Parameter:** `q` (search query) - **Goal:** confirm relevant products come back, and the search actually works ### Step 1 — Set Up the Request ``` GET {{baseUrl}}/products?q=notebook ``` ### Step 2 — Write the Test Script ```javascript pm.test("Search returns products", function () { pm.response.to.have.status(200); let jsonData = pm.response.json(); pm.test("At least one product is returned", () => { pm.expect(jsonData.length).to.be.above(0); }); }); ``` ### Step 3 — Add Dynamic Variables ```javascript pm.environment.set("searchQuery", "notebook"); pm.test("Product names contain the search term", () => { let jsonData = pm.response.json(); let searchTerm = pm.environment.get("searchQuery"); jsonData.forEach(product => { pm.test(product.name + " includes search term", () => { pm.expect(product.name.toLowerCase()).to.include(searchTerm.toLowerCase()); }); }); }); ``` I tested the underlying request logic against JSONPlaceholder as a stand-in (since it doesn't have search, I simulated the loop-assertion pattern against its `/posts` list): ```bash curl -s "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?userId=1" | head -c 300 ``` ```json [{"userId":1,"id":1,"title":"sunt aut facere...","body":"quia et..."},{"userId":1,"id":2,"title":"qui est esse", ... ``` The looping-assertion pattern (`jsonData.forEach(... => pm.test(...))`) works the same way regardless of the underlying data — I loop over the array and assert something about each item individually, which gives me one pass/fail result per item instead of one giant test covering everything at once. ### Step 4 — Run and Inspect I make sure the right environment is active, hit Send, then check the **Tests** tab. > **Note:** I always start with the "happy path" — the simplest, expected-to-succeed scenario — before I add edge cases and negative tests. Trying to write the perfect, fully-loaded test on the first attempt almost always slows me down. --- ## Reading Test Results in Postman | Indicator | Meaning | | --- | --- | | ✅ Green checkmark | Test passed | | ❌ Red X | Test failed — click it for details | | Test count summary | Total passed/failed for the whole request | ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Send Request]:::action --> B{Response Received}:::decision B --> C[Run Test Script]:::script C --> D{Assertions Pass?}:::decision D -->|Yes| E[Green Checkmark ✅]:::pass D -->|No| F[Red X ❌]:::fail classDef action fill:#bbdefb,stroke:#0d47a1,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef decision fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#f57f17,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef script fill:#e1bee7,stroke:#4a148c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef pass fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#1b5e20,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef fail fill:#ffcdd2,stroke:#b71c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` --- ## Debugging: Why Half My Time Goes Here Writing the test is only half the job. The other half — often the harder half — is figuring out *why* a test failed when I genuinely expected it to pass. --- ## The Console Is My Best Friend `console.log()` inside a script is, without exaggeration, the tool I reach for most when something isn't behaving. ```javascript pm.test("Search returns products", function () { let searchTerm = pm.environment.get("searchQuery"); console.log("Search term used: ", searchTerm); let jsonData = pm.response.json(); console.log("Response data: ", jsonData); }); ``` To view it: **View → Show Postman Console** (or the small Console button in the bottom-left). Output appears right after I send a request. > **Note:** I leave `console.log()` statements in during active development, then strip the noisy ones out once a test is stable — a Console full of unrelated logs makes it harder to spot the one line I actually need when debugging something new later. --- ## Isolating the Problem When a script fails, I don't try to fix everything at once. I narrow it down first. | Level | What I Do | | --- | --- | | **Test-level** | Comment out other `pm.test()` blocks, leave only the failing one | | **Request-level** | Send the request *without* the script — does the raw API response look right? | If the raw response is wrong, the problem is the API (or my request). If the raw response is fine but my test still fails, the problem is in my script logic. --- ## Scrutinizing the Response When a test fails unexpectedly, I check three things in order: 1. **Status code** — is it what I expected (200 vs. a surprise 400)? 2. **Response body** — is the JSON structure what I assumed? Are the field names spelled the way I think they are? 3. **Response headers** — sometimes the real clue is hiding here (rate limit info, content-type mismatches, custom error codes) > **Caution:** A surprisingly common bug I've hit: assuming a field name (`user_id` vs `userId` vs `id`) without actually checking the raw response first. I now always `console.log(pm.response.json())` before writing an assertion against a field I haven't personally verified. --- ## Thinking Like a Scientist Debugging, to me, is just running a small experiment: 1. **Form a hypothesis** — "I think the total is wrong because of a missing tax calculation." 2. **Change one thing at a time** — don't alter three variables and the assertion all in the same run. 3. **Ask "what if?"** — try an edge case (empty string, zero, a huge number) and see how the API — and my test — actually respond. --- ## A Full Debugging Walkthrough Here's a real example I like to use when teaching this: testing that an order total is calculated correctly. ```javascript pm.test("Order total is calculated correctly", function () { let price = pm.environment.get("itemPrice"); let quantity = pm.environment.get("quantity"); pm.response.to.have.status(201); let jsonData = pm.response.json(); pm.test("Total matches price * quantity", () => { pm.expect(jsonData.total).to.eql(price * quantity); }); }); ``` ### My Debugging Steps 1. **Add console logs:** ```javascript console.log("price:", price, typeof price); console.log("quantity:", quantity, typeof quantity); console.log("jsonData.total:", jsonData.total); ``` 2. **Check the actual response structure** — does `total` even exist on the object? I run the raw request first: ```bash curl -s -X POST "https://api.example.com/orders" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"itemPrice": 10, "quantity": 3}' ``` 3. **Compare types, not just values.** This is the bug I hit most often in real life: environment variables are stored as *strings*, so `price * quantity` might silently become string concatenation-turned-NaN if I forgot to convert: ```javascript let price = Number(pm.environment.get("itemPrice")); let quantity = Number(pm.environment.get("quantity")); ``` > **Note:** This exact issue — environment variables coming back as strings instead of numbers — has been the root cause of more of my failing tests than almost anything else. I now cast explicitly with `Number()` any time I'm doing arithmetic on a variable pulled from an environment or data file. --- ## Advanced Debugging Tools ### Breakpoints I can click the line number in the Pre-request Script or Tests tab to set a breakpoint (a red dot appears). Running the request pauses execution there, letting me inspect state before continuing — genuinely useful for longer scripts where `console.log()` spam gets unwieldy. ### The Network Tab Below the response area, the **Network** tab shows the raw HTTP traffic — exact headers, raw request body, and the precise response as it went over the wire. I use this when I suspect Postman is sending something subtly different from what I typed (encoding issues, a missing header I assumed was there automatically). ### Monitors for Intermittent Issues If a test fails only sometimes, a scheduled Monitor running the same request periodically helps reveal patterns — is it time-of-day dependent? Environment-specific? A monitor running against staging catching failures that never show up in dev is a strong clue about environment drift. ### Collaborative Debugging A second set of eyes on a shared workspace has caught bugs for me that I'd been staring at for an hour. Sometimes the fix is obvious to someone who didn't write the original script. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Test Fails]:::fail --> B[Console Logs]:::tool A --> C[Isolate: comment out other tests]:::tool A --> D[Check raw response outside script]:::tool B --> E{Bug Found?}:::decision C --> E D --> E E -->|No| F[Breakpoints + Network Tab]:::advanced F --> G{Bug Found?}:::decision G -->|No| H[Ask a Teammate]:::collab E -->|Yes| I[Fix and Re-run]:::success G -->|Yes| I H --> I classDef fail fill:#ffcdd2,stroke:#b71c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef tool fill:#bbdefb,stroke:#0d47a1,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef decision fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#f57f17,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef advanced fill:#e1bee7,stroke:#4a148c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef collab fill:#ffe0b2,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef success fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#1b5e20,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` --- ## Why I Moved to Data-Driven Testing Static, hardcoded tests only ever check one specific case. Real APIs need to handle a huge range of inputs — different usernames, edge-case values, malformed data — and manually writing a separate request for each one doesn't scale. | Benefit | What It Means for Me | | --- | --- | | **Reusability** | One test template runs against many data sets | | **Edge case coverage** | Easy to throw unusual input at the API and see what breaks | | **Realistic scenario coverage** | Mimics the variety of real user input | --- ## CSV vs. JSON as Data Sources | Format | Best For | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | **CSV** | Simple, tabular data | `username,email,password` | | **JSON** | Nested, complex structures | `[{"name": "Alice", "cart": ["item1", "item3"]}]` | A CSV I've actually used for login testing: ```csv username,password,expectedStatus testuser1,password123,true testuser2,badpassword,false ``` --- ## Running Data Through the Collection Runner ### Step 1 — Open the Runner Click the **"..."** next to a Collection's name → **Run Collection**. ### Step 2 — Attach the Data File In the **Data** tab of the runner, I select my CSV or JSON file. Postman shows a preview so I can confirm it parsed correctly before running anything. ### Step 3 — Reference Data in Requests Data file columns become variables automatically: ```json { "username": "{{username}}", "password": "{{password}}" } ``` Tested against a login-style endpoint (using a mock structure, since Reqres's login endpoint expects specific test credentials): ```bash curl -s -X POST "https://reqres.in/api/login" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"email": "eve.holt@reqres.in", "password": "cityslicka"}' ``` Response: ```json { "token": "[REDACTED]" } ``` --- ## Writing Data-Aware Tests The Collection Runner executes the request once per data row, and inside each run, `pm.iterationData` gives me access to that row's values. ```javascript pm.test("Login status matches expected result", function () { let jsonData = pm.response.json(); let expectedStatus = pm.iterationData.get("expectedStatus"); pm.expect(!!jsonData.token).to.eql(expectedStatus === "true"); }); ``` > **Caution:** Values coming from CSV files are always strings — even `"true"` and `"false"` are text, not booleans. I've been bitten by comparing `expectedStatus === true` (a real boolean) against `"true"` (a string) and wondering why the comparison always failed. I now explicitly convert: `expectedStatus === "true"`. ### Data-Driven Assertions, Not Just Inputs Data files aren't only for request bodies — I use them for expected *outputs* too: ```javascript let expectedProductName = pm.iterationData.get("productName"); pm.expect(jsonData.name).to.equal(expectedProductName); ``` This lets a single test script validate dozens of different expected outcomes without any code changes — only the data file changes. --- ## Managing Large Datasets Once a data file grows past a few dozen rows, a few habits keep things maintainable: - **Split by category** — one file per feature area (`login-tests.csv`, `search-tests.csv`) instead of one giant catch-all file - **Run folders, not just single collections** — the Collection Runner can execute an entire folder structure, keeping large test suites organized --- ## Generating Test Data Dynamically Sometimes I don't want static data at all — I want fresh, unique data every run. ```javascript // Generate a random username in a pre-request script let username = "testuser_" + Math.random().toString(36).substring(2, 8); pm.collectionVariables.set("temp_username", username); ``` I tested the randomness logic directly in a Node REPL to confirm the output format: ```javascript > Math.random().toString(36).substring(2, 8) 'k3f9zq' ``` Confirmed — a short, random alphanumeric string, perfect for a disposable test username. ### Libraries for Richer Fake Data For more realistic data (names, addresses, emails), libraries like **Faker.js** or **Chance.js** generate far more convincing test data than a random string ever could. ### Mixing Constant and Variable Data I keep truly constant values (base URL, standard headers) at the Environment or Collection level, and reserve the data file for only what actually changes per test case: ``` {{baseUrl}}/orders/{{orderId}} ``` --- ## Reporting on Data-Driven Results ### Built-In Collection Runner Reporting - **Summary** — overall pass/fail counts across the whole run - **Per-iteration results** — which specific data row passed or failed - **Export Results** — download the full report as JSON or CSV ### Basic Custom Reports With the Visualizer ```javascript pm.test("Store product information for reporting", function () { let jsonData = pm.response.json(); let tableHTML = ""; tableHTML += ``; tableHTML += "
NamePrice
${jsonData.name}${jsonData.price}
"; pm.visualizer.set(tableHTML); }); ``` This renders a simple HTML table in the **Visualizer** tab right after the run — handy for a quick, human-readable summary without leaving Postman. ### Advanced Reporting For genuinely custom reports, I've seen teams: 1. Accumulate results into an array (or environment variable) across iterations 2. Process everything in a script that runs after the full Collection finishes 3. Use templating libraries (Handlebars.js) or charting libraries (Chart.js) to render a polished report > **Note:** For anything I need to track *across* multiple runs over time (not just within one run), the built-in reporting isn't enough — that requires sending results to an external system (a database, a dashboard tool) via a regular HTTP request after the run completes. --- ## The Full Workflow, Visualized Here's how test scripting, debugging, and data-driven testing fit together in my actual day-to-day process: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Write Basic Test Script]:::write --> B[Run Against One Case]:::run B --> C{Passes?}:::decision C -->|No| D[Debug: console.log,
isolate, check response]:::debug D --> B C -->|Yes| E[Attach Data File
CSV/JSON]:::data E --> F[Run via Collection Runner]:::run F --> G{All Iterations Pass?}:::decision G -->|No| H[Inspect Per-Iteration Results]:::debug H --> D G -->|Yes| I[Export/Report Results]:::report classDef write fill:#bbdefb,stroke:#0d47a1,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef run fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#1b5e20,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef decision fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#f57f17,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef debug fill:#ffcdd2,stroke:#b71c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef data fill:#ffe0b2,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef report fill:#e1bee7,stroke:#4a148c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` --- ## Mistakes I Made Along the Way 1. **Assuming JSON field names without checking** — I wrote assertions against `user_id` when the API actually returned `id`. A single `console.log(pm.response.json())` would have saved me twenty minutes. 2. **Comparing strings to booleans/numbers** — environment and data-file variables come back as strings. I now cast explicitly with `Number()` or compare against `"true"`/`"false"` as strings. 3. **Nesting `pm.test()` too deeply** — readable at first, a nightmare to debug three levels in. I keep nesting to one level, maximum. 4. **Not isolating the problem before diving in** — I used to try to fix the whole failing script at once instead of commenting out everything except the one failing assertion. 5. **Treating a single data-driven run as "done"** — I forgot, more than once, to check per-iteration results and only looked at the overall summary, missing that one specific row was quietly failing every time. 6. **No plan for long-term reporting** — early on, I never exported results, so I had no record of whether a flaky test had actually gotten better or worse over time. > **Caution:** Before trusting a "the API is broken" conclusion, I always double-check my own script logic first — genuinely more of my "API bugs" turned out to be a mistake in my test script than an actual server-side problem. --- ## Wrapping Up Test scripts, debugging, and data-driven testing aren't really three separate skills — they're one connected loop. I write an assertion, it fails for a reason I don't expect, I debug it with the console and isolation techniques, and once it's solid, I generalize it into something that runs against dozens of data rows instead of just one. If you're just starting with this part of Postman, my honest suggestion: write one `pm.test()` checking a status code, get comfortable with `console.log()` when it doesn't behave, and only then reach for a CSV file and the Collection Runner. Trying to learn all three at once is exactly what made this feel overwhelming for me the first time around. ### Additional Resources I Actually Use - [Postman Sandbox API Reference](https://learning.postman.com/docs/writing-scripts/script-references/postman-sandbox-api-reference/) - [Postman Assertions Cheatsheet](https://learning.postman.com/docs/writing-scripts/test-scripts/#assertions) - [Postman Help Center: Debugging](https://support.postman.com/hc/en-us/sections/1500008254862-Debugging) - [Postman: Network Tab in Detail](https://learning.postman.com/docs/sending-requests/capturing-request-data/network-tab/) - [Postman: Using Data Files for Tests](https://learning.postman.com/docs/running-collections/working-with-data-files/) - [Chai.js Assertion Library](https://www.chaijs.com/) - [Faker.js on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/faker) --- *Thanks for reading — if you want to practice this end to end, take one existing test you've written, deliberately break something in the response you're asserting against, and walk yourself through debugging it using only `console.log()` and isolation. Once you can find that bug quickly and calmly, turning the same test into a data-driven one is a small, natural next step.*

# Security Testing Is Not a Secret Club: Threat Modeling, STRIDE, DREAD and a Security Mindset For years I assumed security testing belonged to someone else. I pictured people in dark rooms chaining together obscure exploits, and I filed the whole field under "needs superhuman technical skills, not for me." That assumption was wrong, and it kept me from contributing to something I care about. Security testing *does* involve deep technical knowledge at the expert end, but at its core it is the same job I already do as a tester: understand a system, find the risks that threaten its quality, rank them, and reduce them. The only difference is the quality characteristics in the spotlight, which here are **security** and **privacy**. In this post I'll show you how I reuse skills I already had (modeling, risk analysis, heuristics, exploratory testing, automation) to start doing useful security testing. I'll cover threat modeling with data flow diagrams, the STRIDE heuristic, threat trees, DREAD prioritization, and how to thread a security mindset through design sessions, exploratory testing, and pipelines. > [!NOTE] > **How the code here was verified.** The Python scripts were run on Python 3.12 using only the standard library, and the output blocks are real. They target a tiny deliberately weak service that binds to `127.0.0.1`. Commands for third-party tools (Burp Suite, SpotBugs, Dependency-Check) are described from standard usage and are marked **Not run here**, because I couldn't execute them in my environment. > [!CAUTION] > **Only test systems you own or have explicit written permission to test.** Probing someone else's login page, even gently, can be illegal and can lock real people out. Everything in this post is designed for your own machine or a dedicated test environment. ## Table of contents 1. [The big picture](#1-the-big-picture) 2. [Threat modeling in three steps](#2-threat-modeling-in-three-steps) 3. [Step 1: model the system with a data flow diagram](#3-step-1-model-the-system-with-a-data-flow-diagram) 4. [Step 2: find threats with STRIDE](#4-step-2-find-threats-with-stride) 5. [Step 3: dig deeper with threat trees](#5-step-3-dig-deeper-with-threat-trees) 6. [Prioritizing with likelihood, severity and DREAD](#6-prioritizing-with-likelihood-severity-and-dread) 7. [Security in API design sessions](#7-security-in-api-design-sessions) 8. [Exploratory security testing](#8-exploratory-security-testing) 9. [Automation: static analysis and dependency checks](#9-automation-static-analysis-and-dependency-checks) 10. [Security across the whole strategy](#10-security-across-the-whole-strategy) 11. [Cheat sheet and summary](#11-cheat-sheet-and-summary) --- ## 1. The big picture Here's how the pieces fit together. Threat modeling sits in the middle and feeds everything else. ```mermaid flowchart LR M[Model the system
data flow diagram]:::model --> S[Apply STRIDE
high-level threats]:::stride S --> T[Threat trees
concrete attacks]:::tree T --> P[Prioritize
likelihood x severity, or DREAD]:::prio P --> D[API design sessions
bake security in]:::act P --> E[Exploratory charters
probe for real issues]:::act P --> A[Automation
scanners in the pipeline]:::act D -.-> M E -.-> M A -.-> M classDef model fill:#DBEAFE,stroke:#2563EB,color:#1E3A8A classDef stride fill:#FEF3C7,stroke:#D97706,color:#78350F classDef tree fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#14532D classDef prio fill:#FCE7F3,stroke:#DB2777,color:#831843 classDef act fill:#EDE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#4C1D95,stroke-width:2px ``` The dotted lines matter. Every discovery should loop back to improve the model, so the model gets better over time instead of going stale in a wiki page. ### Why this is more accessible than it looks | Security activity | The testing skill it reuses | |---|---| | Threat modeling | Modeling a system to understand it | | Prioritizing threats | Risk analysis (likelihood and severity) | | STRIDE | Heuristics and mnemonics | | Security charters | Exploratory testing | | Dependency and static scanning | Automated checks as change indicators | | Threat modeling in design sessions | Collaborative API design discussions | If you've done any of the left-hand column, you've already done the right. --- ## 2. Threat modeling in three steps A threat model is just a structured way to answer: *what are we protecting, and what could go wrong?* I follow three steps: 1. **Create a model** of the system I can analyze. 2. **Analyze the model** for high-level threats. 3. **Deep-dive** into each threat with a threat tree. My example throughout is a small booking API. The slice I'll model is a single endpoint: `GET /booking/`, which should only be available to admin users. > [!TIP] > Don't model the whole system at once. Small slices are easier to digest, and you'll often spot issues that would be invisible in a sprawling diagram. --- ## 3. Step 1: model the system with a data flow diagram Security cares about *data*: where sensitive information lives, how it moves, and which processes touch it. That's why most threat models use a **data flow diagram (DFD)**. In a classic DFD, each symbol has a meaning: | Element | What it represents | Example in my slice | |---|---|---| | **External entity** | A person or system outside my control that interacts with mine | Admin user | | **Process** | Something that transforms or handles data | Booking API, Auth API | | **Data store** (asset) | Data I want to protect at rest | Bookings, session tokens | | **Data flow** | Data moving between elements | Request with token, token validation | | **Trust boundary / untrusted input** | Where untrusted data enters | The token sent in the request | Here's the flow for `GET /booking/`: 1. The admin sends a request carrying a login token. 2. The booking API extracts the token and sends it to the auth API for validation. 3. If the token confirms admin access, booking details come back. Otherwise the response is a forbidden status. ```mermaid flowchart LR Admin[Admin
external entity]:::entity Token{{Token
untrusted input}}:::untrusted BookAPI((Booking API)):::process AuthAPI((Auth API)):::process Sessions[(Session tokens)]:::asset Bookings[(Bookings)]:::asset Admin -- 1. GET /booking/ + token --> Token Token --> BookAPI BookAPI -- 2. validate token --> AuthAPI AuthAPI <--> Sessions AuthAPI -- 3. valid or forbidden --> BookAPI BookAPI <--> Bookings BookAPI -- bookings or 403 --> Admin classDef entity fill:#DBEAFE,stroke:#2563EB,color:#1E3A8A,stroke-width:2px classDef untrusted fill:#FEE2E2,stroke:#DC2626,color:#7F1D1D,stroke-width:2px classDef process fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#14532D,stroke-width:2px classDef asset fill:#FEF3C7,stroke:#D97706,color:#78350F,stroke-width:2px ``` Drawing this forces useful questions. Who exactly is the external entity? What happens if the token is forged? Which store is most sensitive? The diagram doesn't answer them, but it makes them hard to avoid. > [!NOTE] > A DFD isn't the only option. It focuses on data, so it won't show frameworks or infrastructure. If those matter to your threats, try another model, or add notes to the DFD. The goal is a diagram that *triggers ideas* about what could go wrong. **Try it yourself:** pick a small slice of your own application and draw its DFD. Ask a teammate to fill in the gaps. Disagreements are valuable data. --- ## 4. Step 2: find threats with STRIDE One reason security feels intimidating is the sheer variety of threats and attackers, from criminals selling stolen data to activists taking sites offline. **STRIDE** is a mnemonic that tames this by giving me six categories to walk through, the same way heuristics guided my exploratory testing. ```mermaid mindmap root((STRIDE)) S Spoofing Impersonating a user or system Stolen or forged credentials T Tampering Modifying data or code Man in the middle on a network R Repudiation Denying having acted Missing or falsifiable logs I Information disclosure Leaks to unauthorized people Weak access controls D Denial of service Making a service unavailable Flooding or locking out E Elevation of privilege Horizontal: other users' accounts Vertical: becoming admin ``` ### What each letter means | Letter | Threat | Plain-English question I ask | Example | |---|---|---|---| | **S** | Spoofing | Can someone pretend to be someone they're not? | Presenting a stolen login token | | **T** | Tampering | Can data or code be changed without permission? | Altering a request in transit | | **R** | Repudiation | Could an attacker deny what they did, or could we fail to notice? | No logging on the auth service | | **I** | Information disclosure | Can data reach people who shouldn't see it? | Unencrypted bookings leaked from a backup | | **D** | Denial of service | Can someone stop legitimate users getting in? | Flooding the auth API | | **E** | Elevation of privilege | Can someone gain more access than intended? | A guest reaching admin functions | The categories combine. Spoofing might be the way in, and information disclosure the payoff. That interplay is what makes security testing tricky: a weakness in one part of the system can have a big impact somewhere else. ### Applying STRIDE to my DFD I walk the diagram element by element and ask which letters apply. For my slice, I might conclude: - **Spoofing:** the admin entity could be spoofed. The token might come from an attacker instead of the real admin. - **Denial of service:** both the booking and auth APIs could be targeted. Auth is especially critical, because if it goes down, much of the system becomes inaccessible. - **Repudiation:** if someone tampers with or spoofs tokens, the lack of logging and monitoring in the auth API means the attack might never be noticed or attributed. - **Information disclosure:** bookings are unencrypted at rest, so stolen data would be trivial to read. ### A tested helper: STRIDE-per-element A common refinement is "STRIDE-per-element," which says not every letter applies to every symbol. External entities are mainly subject to spoofing and repudiation, data stores to tampering, repudiation, disclosure and denial of service, and so on. This tiny script applies that mapping to my DFD so I don't forget a category: ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Suggest STRIDE threat categories for each element of a DFD. Uses the common 'STRIDE-per-element' mapping so no category is forgotten.""" S, T, R, I, D, E = "Spoofing", "Tampering", "Repudiation", "Information disclosure", \ "Denial of service", "Elevation of privilege" APPLIES = { "external_entity": [S, R], "process": [S, T, R, I, D, E], "data_store": [T, R, I, D], "data_flow": [T, I, D], } DFD = [ # (element name, element type) for GET /booking/ ("Admin", "external_entity"), ("Booking API", "process"), ("Auth API", "process"), ("Bookings", "data_store"), ("Session tokens", "data_store"), ("Token in request", "data_flow"), ("Token validation call", "data_flow"), ] def analyse(dfd): for name, kind in dfd: for threat in APPLIES[kind]: yield name, kind, threat if __name__ == "__main__": rows = list(analyse(DFD)) for name, kind, threat in rows: print(f"{name:<22}{kind:<17}{threat}") print(f"\n{len(rows)} candidate threats to review") ``` Real output (trimmed to the first few lines and the last line): ```text Admin external_entity Spoofing Admin external_entity Repudiation Booking API process Spoofing Booking API process Tampering Booking API process Repudiation ... Token validation call data_flow Information disclosure Token validation call data_flow Denial of service 28 candidate threats to review ``` > [!NOTE] > 28 candidates from seven elements looks like a lot, and that's the point. This is a *checklist of questions*, not a list of confirmed vulnerabilities. Most candidates will be dismissed quickly ("this flow is internal and encrypted"); the value is in the few that make the team go quiet. **Try it yourself:** label each element of your DFD with the STRIDE letters that might apply, then discuss how you currently mitigate each one. --- ## 5. Step 3: dig deeper with threat trees STRIDE categories are broad. "Spoofing" tells me *what kind* of problem to worry about, but not *how* it could happen. A **threat tree** (or attack tree) breaks a threat down from abstract to concrete, level by level. ### Spoofing an admin ```mermaid flowchart TB Root[Spoof an admin user]:::root Root --> G[Guess credentials]:::l1 Root --> C[Steal credentials or tokens]:::l1 Root --> SE[Social engineering]:::l1 G --> G1[Default or weak password]:::l2 G --> G2[Brute force with common password list]:::l2 C --> C1[Token leaked in error messages]:::l2 C --> C2[Token leaked by a third-party tool]:::l2 C --> C3[Token sniffed over unencrypted HTTP]:::l2 SE --> SE1[Phishing the admin]:::l2 SE --> SE2[Pretending to be support]:::l2 classDef root fill:#7F1D1D,stroke:#450A0A,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px classDef l1 fill:#FCA5A5,stroke:#DC2626,color:#450A0A classDef l2 fill:#FEF2F2,stroke:#EF4444,color:#7F1D1D ``` ### Denial of service Threat trees capture variety, too. A DoS tree includes the familiar distributed flood, but also self-inflicted routes such as misconfiguration, for example accidentally leaving a management endpoint publicly reachable that can switch a service off. (Spring Boot's actuator module is one example of a framework feature that can be exposed this way if not locked down.) ```mermaid flowchart TB Root[Take the service offline]:::root Root --> F[Flood with requests]:::l1 Root --> M[Abuse misconfiguration]:::l1 Root --> L[Lock out legitimate users]:::l1 F --> F1[Distributed flood across many sources]:::l2 F --> F2[Expensive requests that tie up resources]:::l2 M --> M1[Public management endpoint can shut service down]:::l2 M --> M2[Debug features left enabled]:::l2 L --> L1[Trigger account lockouts on purpose]:::l2 L --> L2[Ransomware on a host]:::l2 classDef root fill:#1E3A8A,stroke:#172554,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px classDef l1 fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#2563EB,color:#172554 classDef l2 fill:#EFF6FF,stroke:#3B82F6,color:#1E3A8A ``` > [!WARNING] > Notice that a lockout policy appears in the DoS tree as an *attack route*. Defenses create new attack surface. If an attacker can deliberately trigger lockouts for an admin, the "fix" for brute forcing becomes a DoS weapon. Mitigations deserve their own threat analysis. ### Habits for good threat trees - **Build them collaboratively.** Different people imagine different attacks. - **Research how others were attacked.** Public write-ups from security researchers are a goldmine. - **Check known vulnerabilities in your own tools and libraries**, and ask how each could be used against you. - **Let your imagination run.** Pruning comes later during prioritization. --- ## 6. Prioritizing with likelihood, severity and DREAD A threat is just a particular kind of risk, so I can prioritize it like any other: by **likelihood** and **severity**. High likelihood plus high severity means mitigate first. ```mermaid quadrantChart title Prioritizing threats x-axis Low likelihood --> High likelihood y-axis Low severity --> High severity quadrant-1 Mitigate first quadrant-2 Plan and monitor quadrant-3 Accept or revisit later quadrant-4 Cheap fixes Weak admin password: [0.9, 0.85] Exposed actuator endpoint: [0.6, 0.8] SQL injection: [0.35, 0.9] Unencrypted bookings: [0.25, 0.55] Verbose error pages: [0.7, 0.25] ``` *These placements are illustrative. Your team's context decides where each threat lands.* ### DREAD for finer-grained scoring DREAD, a technique promoted by OWASP and originally from Microsoft, scores each threat from 1 to 10 on five dimensions and averages them: | Letter | Question | Higher score means | |---|---|---| | **D**amage | How bad is the harm to us and our users? | More damage | | **R**eproducibility | How easily can an attacker repeat it? | Easier to repeat | | **E**xploitability | How easy is it to carry out? | Easier to exploit | | **A**ffected users | How many people are hit? | More users | | **D**iscoverability | How easy is it for an attacker to find? | Easier to find | The worked example is a SQL injection that reveals privileged data: | Dimension | Score | Reason | |---|---|---| | Damage | 7 | Hidden sensitive data could be revealed | | Reproducibility | 8 | Once found, it's easy to repeat | | Exploitability | 3 | Needs strong SQL injection skills and knowledge of the database structure | | Affected users | 10 | Losing the database affects everyone | | Discoverability | 8 | Injection probes against the APIs could reveal it | Add them up (7 + 8 + 3 + 10 + 8 = 36) and divide by five: **7.2**. ### A tested DREAD calculator ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Score and rank threats with DREAD (average of five 1-10 scores).""" from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Threat: name: str damage: int reproducibility: int exploitability: int affected_users: int discoverability: int def __post_init__(self): for field, value in vars(self).items(): if field != "name" and not 1 <= value <= 10: raise ValueError(f"{field} must be 1-10, got {value}") @property def score(self) -> float: total = (self.damage + self.reproducibility + self.exploitability + self.affected_users + self.discoverability) return round(total / 5, 1) def rank(threats): return sorted(threats, key=lambda t: t.score, reverse=True) if __name__ == "__main__": threats = [ Threat("SQL injection reveals data", 7, 8, 3, 10, 8), # the worked example: 7.2 Threat("Admin password brute-forced", 9, 9, 8, 10, 9), Threat("Actuator endpoint shuts service down", 6, 9, 7, 10, 5), Threat("Bookings stored unencrypted", 6, 4, 3, 8, 3), ] print(f"{'Score':<7}Threat") for t in rank(threats): print(f"{t.score:<7}{t.name}") ``` Real output: ```text Score Threat 9.0 Admin password brute-forced 7.4 Actuator endpoint shuts service down 7.2 SQL injection reveals data 4.8 Bookings stored unencrypted ``` The first threat reproduces the 7.2 from the worked example. The scores for the other three are numbers I made up to demonstrate ranking; they aren't measurements of anything. I also added input validation, so a score of 11 raises an error rather than silently skewing results (I tested that too). > [!CAUTION] > DREAD looks objective, but every number is a judgment call. Two people can score the same threat very differently, and "Discoverability" is especially slippery, since assuming attackers won't find something is risky. Some teams avoid DREAD for that reason. I treat it as a conversation starter: the *discussion* about why we disagree on a score is where the learning happens. Score as a group, and write down the reasoning. --- ## 7. Security in API design sessions Threat modeling works best as a team activity, and the natural place for it is the API design discussion. In those sessions the team already aims to understand why a feature is being built, make sure everyone shares the same picture, and capture risks before coding starts. Threats are just one more kind of risk to capture. The payoff is that security gets **baked in** rather than bolted on. A concrete example: while discussing a password reset feature, someone realizes an attacker could repeatedly trigger resets to lock a victim out of their account. The team adds a confirmation email step and a time limit on reset links *before* the feature ships, which is far cheaper than retrofitting after an incident. You don't need a full threat model for every change. I use a simple rule of thumb: | Change type | My threat modeling depth | |---|---| | Touches authentication, authorization, or personal data | Full session with a DFD and STRIDE | | New endpoint with sensitive output | Quick STRIDE pass on an existing diagram | | Cosmetic or low-risk change | Skip it, or just ask "what could go wrong?" | | Existing feature revisited | Update the previous model rather than starting over | > [!TIP] > Keep your models in version control next to the code (a Mermaid diagram in the repo works nicely). Iterating on an old model is much faster than starting from a blank page, and it builds the habit. --- ## 8. Exploratory security testing Threat models are abstract: they say what *could* happen. To find out what *does* happen in the real product, I use exploratory testing: time-boxed, charter-driven sessions focused on a specific risk, just with security as the topic. ### Where charters come from 1. **My threat trees.** Pick a leaf and turn it into a charter. 2. **The OWASP Top 10.** It lists the most common web application threats and gives me a different perspective from my own model. A threat model is only as good as the people who built it, and the Top 10 helps make sure the gaps I leave aren't the most common ones. Not every entry applies to every product. Cross-site scripting, for example, is moot for an API with no front end to render it. I pick the relevant ones. A charter inspired by *Identification and Authentication Failures* looks like this: ```text Explore the auth API With a list of common passwords and a testing tool To discover whether a password can be brute forced ``` ### Running the charter with a tool (Burp Suite) > [!NOTE] > **Not run here.** The steps below describe standard Burp Suite Community Edition usage. Menu names can differ between versions, so check the current documentation. 1. Start the application under test (the whole system, or just the auth service). 2. Open Burp Suite Community Edition and use a temporary project with default settings. 3. In **Intruder → Target**, set the host and port of the application. 4. In **Positions**, paste a login request and mark only the password value as the position to vary: ```http POST /auth/login HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8080 Content-Type: application/json { "username": "admin", "password": "fuzzme" } ``` 5. In **Payloads**, choose a *Simple list* and paste in a list of common passwords. 6. Start the attack and review the status codes returned for each attempt. > [!WARNING] > **Port clash.** Burp Suite's built-in proxy listens on port 8080 by default, the same port many local web apps use. If you open your app and see a Burp response, change or disable the proxy listener (or move the app to another port) and restart. Paid and free alternatives exist; OWASP ZAP is an open-source option with a steeper learning curve. ### A tested, safe equivalent you can run on your own machine Because I can't hand you a vulnerable system to point Burp at, I built a deliberately weak local login service and a tiny charter script. The service listens only on `127.0.0.1`. It accepts `admin` / `password` and, in its default "weak" mode, never limits attempts. Started with `--hardened`, it locks an account after 5 consecutive failures and sets protective cookie flags. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """A deliberately weak local login service for practising security checks. Run it with --hardened to see the same checks pass. Binds to 127.0.0.1 only. Never expose it, and never reuse these ideas as real auth.""" import json, sys, time from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer HARDENED = "--hardened" in sys.argv MAX_FAILS, LOCK_SECONDS = 5, 30 fails = {} # username -> (count, locked_until) class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def _send(self, code, body, cookie=None): data = json.dumps(body).encode() self.send_response(code) self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json") self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data))) if cookie: self.send_header("Set-Cookie", cookie) self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(data) def do_POST(self): if self.path != "/auth/login": return self._send(404, {}) creds = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"]))) user, now = creds.get("username"), time.time() count, locked_until = fails.get(user, (0, 0)) if HARDENED and now < locked_until: return self._send(429, {"error": "too many attempts"}) if creds.get("username") == "admin" and creds.get("password") == "password": [REDACTED], None) flags = "; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict" if HARDENED else "" return self._send(200, {"ok": True}, cookie=f"token=abc123; Path=/{flags}") count += 1 fails[user] = (count, now + LOCK_SECONDS if count >= MAX_FAILS else 0) self._send(403, {"error": "bad credentials"}) def log_message(self, *a): pass if __name__ == "__main__": ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8090), Handler).serve_forever() ``` And the charter script. It tries a short list of common passwords, tallies the status codes, and reports findings. It **refuses to run against anything except localhost**, which is a guardrail I'd recommend building into any practice tooling: ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Charter: explore the auth API with a short common-password list to learn whether a password can be brute forced. LOCALHOST ONLY by design.""" import json, sys, urllib.request, urllib.error from collections import Counter from urllib.parse import urlparse PASSWORDS = ["123456", "admin", "letmein", "password", "qwerty", "welcome", "iloveyou", "monkey", "dragon", "football"] def attempt(url, user, pw): req = urllib.request.Request(url, method="POST", data=json.dumps({"username": user, "password": pw}).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}) try: with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as r: return r.status except urllib.error.HTTPError as e: return e.code def run(url, user="admin"): host = urlparse(url).hostname if host not in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1"): sys.exit("Refusing to run: this practice script only targets localhost.") codes, cracked = Counter(), None for pw in PASSWORDS: code = attempt(url, user, pw) codes[code] += 1 if code == 200 and cracked is None: cracked = pw print("status codes seen:", dict(codes)) findings = [] if cracked: findings.append(f"weak credential accepted: '{cracked}'") if not any(c in codes for c in (429, 423)): findings.append("no lockout or rate limiting observed") print("FINDINGS:" if findings else "No findings from this session.") for f in findings: print(" -", f) return findings if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(1 if run(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "http://127.0.0.1:8090/auth/login") else 0) ``` **Run against the weak service (real output):** ```text status codes seen: {403: 9, 200: 1} FINDINGS: - weak credential accepted: 'password' - no lockout or rate limiting observed ``` **Run against the `--hardened` service (real output):** ```text status codes seen: {403: 8, 200: 1, 429: 1} FINDINGS: - weak credential accepted: 'password' ``` **Pointed at a non-local address (real output):** ```text Refusing to run: this practice script only targets localhost. ``` Two lessons jump out of those results: 1. The weak service reproduces the same two findings an exploratory session would surface: an easily guessed default credential, and no control that slows or stops guessing. Every wrong guess just returned `403`, never anything that suggested the system was pushing back. 2. The hardened service *did* start returning `429` after repeated failures, but the weak password **still worked**, because `password` was only the fourth guess, before the lockout threshold. A lockout is not a substitute for strong credentials. Both fixes are needed. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor Tester participant API as Auth API (weak) participant H as Auth API (hardened) rect rgb(254, 226, 226) Note over Tester,API: Weak service Tester->>API: login with 123456 API-->>Tester: 403 Tester->>API: login with admin / letmein API-->>Tester: 403 Tester->>API: login with password API-->>Tester: 200 (weak default accepted) Tester->>API: keep guessing API-->>Tester: 403 only, never throttled end rect rgb(220, 252, 231) Note over Tester,H: Hardened service Tester->>H: same guesses H-->>Tester: 403 for wrong guesses H-->>Tester: 200 for the weak default Tester->>H: five failures in a row H-->>Tester: 429 too many attempts end ``` ### Cookie flags: another quick check The chapter's static analysis tool flagged cookies set without the `HttpOnly` and `Secure` flags. I wrote a small check for that same class of issue, which inspects the `Set-Cookie` header from a login response: ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Check a login response's Set-Cookie header for HttpOnly / Secure / SameSite. The same class of issue static analysis flagged in the chapter.""" import json, sys, urllib.request def check_cookie(header: str): parts = [p.strip() for p in header.split(";")] attrs = {p.split("=")[0].lower() for p in parts[1:]} return [msg for flag, msg in (("httponly", "missing HttpOnly: scripts can read it"), ("secure", "missing Secure: may travel over plain HTTP"), ("samesite", "missing SameSite: weaker CSRF protection")) if flag not in attrs] if __name__ == "__main__": url = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "http://127.0.0.1:8090/auth/login" req = urllib.request.Request(url, method="POST", data=json.dumps({"username": "admin", "password": "password"}).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r: header = r.headers.get("Set-Cookie", "") problems = check_cookie(header) print("Set-Cookie:", header) print("\n".join(" - " + p for p in problems) if problems else "cookie flags look good") sys.exit(1 if problems else 0) ``` Against the weak service: ```text Set-Cookie: token=abc123; Path=/ - missing HttpOnly: scripts can read it - missing Secure: may travel over plain HTTP - missing SameSite: weaker CSRF protection ``` Against the hardened service: ```text Set-Cookie: token=abc123; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict cookie flags look good ``` Both scripts exit with `1` when they find something and `0` when they don't, so they can be dropped into a CI job. > [!NOTE] > **What these flags do.** `HttpOnly` stops page scripts from reading the cookie, which limits damage from script injection. `Secure` tells browsers to send it only over HTTPS. `SameSite` restricts cross-site sending, which helps against cross-site request forgery. Whether a cookie is even the right mechanism for your API depends on how clients authenticate. ### More charter ideas | Area to explore | Idea | STRIDE link | |---|---|---| | Message endpoint | Send content that looks like SQL to see how input is handled | Tampering, Information disclosure | | Booking listing | Vary the `roomid` query string with unexpected values | Information disclosure, Elevation of privilege | | Login payload | Send malformed or oversized bodies, watch for server errors and stack traces | Denial of service, Information disclosure | | Admin-only endpoint | Call it with no token, an expired token, and a regular user's token | Spoofing, Elevation of privilege | > [!CAUTION] > Even on your own systems, think before you fuzz. Injection probes can corrupt data or crash services. Use a disposable environment with throwaway data, and take a note of what you did so you can reproduce and explain it. --- ## 9. Automation: static analysis and dependency checks Exploratory sessions are one-off and human. But vulnerabilities also *appear over time*: a library I use gets a newly disclosed flaw, or a pattern I relied on turns out to be unsafe. Automation helps me notice those changes, the same way regression checks tell me when behavior changes. ```mermaid flowchart LR C[Commit code]:::start --> SA[Static analysis
scan my code]:::tool C --> DC[Dependency check
scan my libraries]:::tool SA --> R{Findings?}:::decision DC --> R R -- yes --> F[Fix, upgrade, or
record a decision]:::fix R -- no --> D([Deploy]):::ok F --> C NEW[New vulnerability
published later]:::alert -.-> DC classDef start fill:#E0E7FF,stroke:#4F46E5,color:#312E81 classDef tool fill:#CFFAFE,stroke:#0891B2,color:#164E63 classDef decision fill:#FEF3C7,stroke:#D97706,color:#78350F classDef fix fill:#FEE2E2,stroke:#DC2626,color:#7F1D1D classDef ok fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#14532D classDef alert fill:#F3E8FF,stroke:#9333EA,color:#581C87 ``` ### Static analysis Static analysis inspects code without running it. For a Java/Maven project, one combination is **SpotBugs** with the **Find Security Bugs** plugin. Added to the project's `pom.xml`: > [!NOTE] > **Not run here.** I couldn't execute Maven. The versions below are the ones used in the source chapter, which is several years old. **Check for current versions before using them.** ```xml com.github.spotbugs spotbugs-maven-plugin 4.5.0.0 com.h3xstream.findsecbugs findsecbugs-plugin 1.10.1 ``` Running `mvn spotbugs:check` analyzes the code and lists warnings. The chapter's run reported two medium-severity items about a cookie set without the HttpOnly flag and without the secure flag, which is exactly the class of problem my `cookie_check.py` looks for at runtime. Static analysis finds it in source; the runtime check confirms what actually goes over the wire. Having both is stronger than either. ### Dependency checking Modern software is mostly other people's code. **OWASP Dependency-Check** scans project dependencies against databases of known vulnerabilities and can run locally, before code is pushed, which suits teams who don't want to depend only on a hosting platform's scanner. Added to `pom.xml`: ```xml org.owasp dependency-check-maven 6.5.0 check ``` Running `mvn verify` produces a report at `target/dependency-check-report.html`. In the chapter's example it flagged a critical vulnerability in the `jackson-databind` library, and the fix was to upgrade to a patched version. ### What automation can and can't do | Tool type | Good at | Blind spots | |---|---|---| | Static analysis | Insecure patterns in my own code | Logic flaws, business rules, runtime configuration | | Dependency scanning | Known flaws in libraries | Unknown (zero-day) flaws, flaws in my own code | | Scripted runtime checks | Specific, repeatable issues (cookie flags, lockouts) | Anything I didn't think to check | | Scanners in a pipeline | Fast, consistent feedback | Context: they can't judge what matters to *my* users | > [!CAUTION] > **Green doesn't mean secure.** Automated security scans, like automated regression checks, won't find every problem. A clean report is evidence about the things the tool knows to look for, nothing more. Don't let it lull you into a false sense of security. > [!TIP] > Triage scanner output rather than blindly chasing zero findings. Some warnings won't apply to how you use a library. Record those decisions with reasons so the next person doesn't redo the analysis. --- ## 10. Security across the whole strategy The final lesson is the one I find most freeing: security isn't a separate discipline I must master before contributing. It's a *mindset* applied across everything I already do. ```mermaid flowchart TB SM([Security mindset]):::core SM --> A[Design discussions
threat model together, bake in mitigations]:::a SM --> B[Exploratory testing
security charters from threats and the Top 10]:::b SM --> C[Automation
static analysis, dependency scans, runtime checks]:::c SM --> D[Risk analysis
likelihood x severity or DREAD]:::d SM --> E[Monitoring and logging
so repudiation isn't free for attackers]:::e classDef core fill:#111827,stroke:#111827,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px classDef a fill:#DBEAFE,stroke:#2563EB,color:#1E3A8A classDef b fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#14532D classDef c fill:#FEF3C7,stroke:#D97706,color:#78350F classDef d fill:#FCE7F3,stroke:#DB2777,color:#831843 classDef e fill:#EDE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#4C1D95 ``` Here's a realistic starter plan for a team that has done none of this before: ```mermaid timeline title Getting started with security testing Week 1 : Draw a DFD for one small slice : Walk through STRIDE as a team Week 2 : Build a threat tree for the scariest threat : Score the threats and agree on the top three Week 3 : Write one security charter and run it on a test environment : Fix or log what you find Week 4 : Add a dependency check to the pipeline : Add one scripted runtime check Ongoing : Update the model when designs change : Re-run charters after significant releases ``` ### Common mistakes | Mistake | Why it hurts | Better approach | |---|---|---| | Thinking security needs hacker-level skills before you start | Nobody starts, and risks go unexamined | Start with modeling and risk analysis you already know | | Modeling the whole system at once | Overwhelming, and details get missed | Model small slices and iterate | | Doing threat modeling alone | One perspective, many gaps | Make it collaborative | | Treating scanner results as the whole story | False confidence | Combine scanners with modeling and exploration | | Trusting DREAD numbers literally | Scores are subjective | Use scoring as a discussion aid | | Fixing a threat without analyzing the fix | Mitigations can create new threats (such as lockout-based DoS) | Threat-model your mitigations | | Testing systems without permission | Legal and ethical risk | Only test what you own or are authorized to test | | Ignoring logging | Attacks go unnoticed and unprovable | Treat repudiation as a real threat | --- ## 11. Cheat sheet and summary | Topic | Remember | |---|---| | **Mindset** | Security testing reuses modeling, risk analysis, exploratory testing and automation | | **Threat model steps** | Model, apply STRIDE, build threat trees | | **DFD symbols** | External entities, processes, data stores, data flows, untrusted input | | **STRIDE** | Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege | | **Threat trees** | Break a broad threat into concrete attacks, level by level | | **Prioritization** | Likelihood x severity, or DREAD (average of five 1-10 scores) | | **Design sessions** | Threat model together so mitigations are built in | | **Charters** | Draw from threat trees and the OWASP Top 10 | | **Automation** | Static analysis and dependency checks, plus small scripted runtime checks | | **Warning** | Scanners don't find everything; always have permission to test | ### Summary If you remember only a few things from this post, let them be these. Security testing isn't a secret club. It's the testing you already do, aimed at security and privacy risks. Start by modeling a small slice of your system as a data flow diagram so you can see where valuable data lives and where untrusted data enters. Walk it with STRIDE so you don't overlook a whole category of threat, then use threat trees to turn vague worries into concrete attacks. Rank those threats using likelihood and severity or DREAD, treating the numbers as a way to start discussion rather than end it. Then spread the mindset: discuss threats in design sessions so fixes are built in, run charter-based exploratory sessions to see what is really true of your running system, and add scanners and scripted checks to your pipeline so you hear about new problems early. Remember that no tool gives you a guarantee, and that every defense deserves the same suspicious eye as the system it protects. You don't need to be a hacker to make your product harder to hack. You need curiosity, a diagram, and a willingness to ask "what could go wrong?" out loud with your team. --- ### Appendix: files in the lab | File | Purpose | Status | |---|---|---| | `stride_per_element.py` | Maps DFD elements to candidate STRIDE threats | Tested | | `dread.py` | DREAD scoring, validation and ranking | Tested | | `mock_auth.py` | Weak (and `--hardened`) local login service on 127.0.0.1:8090 | Tested | | `bruteforce_check.py` | Localhost-only charter script for credential guessing and lockouts | Tested | | `cookie_check.py` | Checks cookie flags in a login response | Tested | | Burp Suite steps, `mvn` commands, `pom.xml` snippets | Standard tool usage from the chapter | Not run here |

files.content:
When we talk about "SQL implementations," we're referring to the specific **Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS)** that use SQL as their standard database language.

While they all share the core SQL standard, each system has its own extensions, performance characteristics, and unique features. Here are the most prominent examples, categorized by their typical use.

### Open-Source & Widely Adopted Workhorses

These are the most common databases powering modern web applications and are completely free to use.

| System | Key Strength & Characteristic | Example SQL Extension / Unique Feature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PostgreSQL** | Extensibility, standards compliance, and advanced features. It can handle not just relational data but also JSON, geospatial data, and vectors. It's known as the "Swiss Army Knife" of databases. | Supports `JSONB` for querying JSON with full indexing. Has a rich catalog of extensions like `PostGIS` for geographic data. Uses `COPY` for fast bulk data loading. |
| **MySQL** | Historically known for raw read speed and reliability. It’s the ‘M’ in the LAMP stack and a cornerstone of the early web. Now owned by Oracle, its open-source fork, **MariaDB**, is a popular drop-in replacement. | Uses backticks `` ` `` for quoting identifiers. The `SHOW` commands (e.g., `SHOW TABLES;`, `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS;`) are a MySQL-specific way to inspect the database. |
| **SQLite** | A serverless, self-contained database engine that stores the entire database as a single file on disk. It's the most deployed database in the world, embedded in every smartphone, browser, and countless applications. | Implements `PRAGMA` commands for database-specific settings. The `REPLACE INTO` syntax is a convenient shortcut for inserting or replacing a row based on a conflict. |

---

### Major Commercial & Enterprise Systems

These are proprietary systems from large technology vendors, designed for massive scale and complex corporate environments.

| System | Key Strength & Characteristic | Example SQL Extension / Unique Feature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Oracle Database** | The dominant force in large enterprise and financial systems for decades. Known for its extreme reliability, extensive feature set, and complex configurability. | Its procedural language, **PL/SQL**, is tightly integrated and powerful. Uses `CONNECT BY` for hierarchical queries. Row-level locking and `FLASHBACK` queries are advanced features. |
| **Microsoft SQL Server** | Deep integration with the Microsoft ecosystem (.NET, Azure, Excel). Valued for its excellent developer tooling, particularly SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). | Its procedural language is **T-SQL (Transact-SQL)** . Uses `TOP` to limit query results instead of the standard `LIMIT`. `SELECT TOP 10 * FROM Customers`. |
| **IBM Db2** | A veteran system running reliably on mainframes (z/OS) as well as Linux/Windows. Designed for extreme transaction processing and data integrity in industries like banking and aviation. | Supports a unique `MERGE` syntax for "upserts." Its native procedural language is SQL PL. Offers advanced time-travel query syntax with `FOR SYSTEM_TIME`. |

---

### Cloud-Native & Specialized Systems

These are modern databases, often born in the cloud, designed for massive scale or specific analytical workloads.

| System | Key Strength & Characteristic | Example SQL Extension / Unique Feature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Google BigQuery** | A serverless, highly scalable data warehouse designed for analyzing petabytes of data using SQL. | Supports `STRUCT` and `ARRAY` data types natively in SQL. You can query data directly from external sources like Google Sheets. Uses backticks for quoting. |
| **Snowflake** | A fully managed cloud data platform that separates compute from storage, allowing many different workloads to run simultaneously without competing for resources. | Supports semi-structured data querying with a `VARIANT` data type. Its `QUALIFY` clause allows you to filter window functions directly in the main query. |
| **Amazon Aurora** | A MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible service from AWS that’s rebuilt for the cloud, offering higher performance and durability by separating the compute and storage layers. | Because it's protocol-compatible, you use standard MySQL or PostgreSQL drivers and SQL syntax, but gain cloud-native features like Aurora Serverless for automatic scaling. |

In essence, while they all speak the same foundational language of `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `JOIN`, their unique dialects and superpowers make them suited for different tasks—from running a high-frequency trading system on Oracle to powering an iPhone app's local storage with SQLite.
